i am grateful, mr president, for the opportunity to greet the port workers, including 100 portuguese workers, who are demonstrating today outside the european parliament and who are staging a strike in several countries of the european union. the port workers are fighting for, among other things, the defence of employment, safety at work, professional qualifications, collective agreements and trade union rights, and are therefore calling for the rejection of the directive on port services, which, after being rejected by the european parliament, has been incomprehensibly reintroduced by the european commission. i therefore call on the european parliament to live up to its responsibilities by rejecting it again.
mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, we welcome the creation of european citizenship because we want a europe of citizens and not just of services, goods and capital. this citizenship has grown with the strengthening of the protection of the rights and interests of the citizens of the member states and the creation of the area of freedom, security and justice. i would like to congratulate commissioner frattini on the work he has been doing in this area. the balance sheet presented by the european commission for the last three years is generally positive. the main problems identified are mainly linked to poor implementation and incorrect practices, rather than to the lack of conformity of national legislation. this reinforces the importance of an information policy on the correct interpretation of union rules and the correct application of citizens' rights and calls for the necessary steps to be taken to make the charter of fundamental rights legally binding. we want to strengthen and consolidate europe's identity and to encourage greater involvement of citizens in the process of european integration, which should translate into higher rates of participation in european elections. less positive is the report by mr catania, which we are debating today, in which about half of the 40 points call into question the very concept of citizenship, advocating the recognition of citizenship of the union irrespective of whether one has the nationality of a member state, which is clearly contrary to what is laid down in the treaty. european citizenship cannot and should not be understood as an intention to create artificially a supranational identity which seeks to replace national feelings. the promotion of awareness of a common heritage based on a set of common traditions and fundamental values must be done with respect for national identity. citizenship of the union is a complementary citizenship which is in addition to national citizenship and does not replace it. to do otherwise is to kill the concept of european citizenship and to create difficulties for the european project.
this debate is important, but even more important are the urgent and effective measures that must be taken to put an end to the serious human rights violation of trafficking in persons, especially women and children, for the purpose of sexual exploitation and forced labour - a veritable slavery. we cannot remain indifferent to the growth of this scourge worldwide, which affects between 600 000 and 800 000 people, 80% of whom are women and children, including here in the european union, where the victims number more than 100 000 a year. this situation is not unrelated to wars, political instability in the countries of origin, the worsening of social and regional inequalities, the feminization of poverty and unemployment, violence against women and children, which calls for new approaches and new integrated policies. it is well known that trafficking for sexual exploitation is directly linked to prostitution, and therefore a set of integrated measures for the protection of the dignity of women and children and against trafficking in human beings and money laundering is urgently needed, which also requires the end of tax havens and economic and social policies that are supportive of and committed to economic and social cohesion.
member of the commission. mr president, in response to the last question – which bears almost no relation whatsoever to the subject matter of this debate – let me say that the honourable member makes a rather good case for russia and ukraine being brought into the wto, because they would be subject to international rules and to the dispute settlement machinery of the wto. however, for them to enjoy that privilege, they have to accept certain undertakings unambiguously beforehand, and that remains the subject of continuing discussion between us. i will try and be brief, but a very large number of points and issues have been raised in this debate. i cannot do them all justice. i welcome the ideas that have been put forward by members. i hear the criticisms that have been expressed about what we have done and needless to say i am grateful for the praise and compliments, but i am only too well aware that praise comes to a negotiator when he does not do anything wrong. the test for the negotiator is for him to do something right. that is harder, and that is the challenge held out before me in the coming months. i am in complete agreement with the member who said that we need to strengthen the rights of the european parliament in relation to trade – i have always said that – and, in the spirit of the times, given that our relationship is going so swimmingly, i cannot think of anything i would rather have than a strengthened relationship between us. a word to those who have expressed concern about the international criticism that has been directed at the european union. it is criticism up to a point, but a better word for it is propaganda. all is fair in love and war in international trade negotiations, and we have to understand that where our negotiating partners arrive at a convergence of interests, notably in respect of agriculture, you will find a cacophony of voices directed against us, all of which have one goal in mind, which is to place pressure on the unity of the 25 member states: to seek to divide the 25 and as a result, find advantage for themselves in the negotiations. that is why the unity that we found in hong kong is so important. it is not just a question of giving ourselves the comfort of solidarity amongst ourselves; unity of argument and message is the best riposte to the propaganda that will be aimed against us. as it happens, my judgement is that whilst the propaganda will not fall away and its decibel count will not go down, whilst those critical voices will maintain their shrillness in years to come, they are becoming less convincing and finding a weaker reception amongst many of the international commentariat who follow these negotiations in detail. i have found, since hong kong, a rather more balanced and nuanced appreciation of the content of these negotiations than i found on previous occasions. but we do not just have to find responses to people’s criticisms and propaganda, as a number of members have quite rightly argued; we also have to reach out and find allies. we are not going to complete this round unless we are able to find some accommodation between ourselves and the interests and negotiating objectives of the g20 group of emerging economies. they are not homogeneous, but they have an effective discipline which i welcome. we would not be able to negotiate as we are; we would not have the prospect of finding a satisfactory outcome if we did not have those g20 countries, the emerging economies organised as they are and brought together as coherently as they are, in these negotiations. i think therefore that post-cancún, yes, it gives us a lot of grief sometimes in the european union to find our negotiating partners so well organised, but on the other hand the opposite of organisation is chaos and chaos is the enemy of a successful trade round. however, just as i welcome our negotiating partners in the g20, i think those members who have pointed out tonight that we need to cement our coalition of interests and our relationship with the acp countries are also correct. one thing i have learned and that has been borne in on me since i took up this post – something that some members might bear in mind, given some of the contributions that have been made this evening – is that when you appeal to, or respond to, or try to accommodate the interests of certain developing countries, more often than not you will find yourself taking away from, or denying opportunities to, or dissatisfying, other developing countries. and so it is the case that when we are criticised, as the commission has been on one or two occasions this evening, for not taking agricultural reform fast enough or far enough for the interests and benefit of certain rather more competitive developing countries, we have to understand that during the course of that reform, the further it goes or the faster it goes, the more pain we will be causing other developing countries to experience. so when i travel around, whether it be in africa or the caribbean, the street demonstrations that i face are not amongst the poor and exploited of the world who want us to go further in agricultural reform; in my experience of street demonstrations it has been people from some very poor, needy and deprived developing countries who are asking us to go slower in our agricultural reform, not faster. to an extent this is a question of compensating developing countries for the adjustment that is necessitated by that agricultural reform. mrs kinnock has quite rightly highlighted the issue of sugar. the commission’s approach – and i say this on behalf of mrs fischer boel as well as myself – is clear. we proposed eur 190 million per year for each year between 2007 and 2013 for our proposed sugar action plan agreed with acp countries. but the compromise that was found on the budget means a 20% reduction of the money that we thought we would have available for that action plan under the relevant heading. that is an unattractive prospect, if we are going to have, through budgetary constraints, to retreat from the original ambition of the plan that we set forward. tonight i invite the european parliament to help the commission ensure that there is enough money to make that action plan a reality and to make sure that it genuinely meets the needs of those sugar-dependent acp countries with whom we have had such an important historical relationship – a relationship we want to carry over as meaningfully to the future – and to help us ensure that that budgetary allocation is sustained. i will certainly be pushing to maintain the original eur 190 million, but we in the commission are not the budgetary authority; you and the council are. therefore i appeal to you to exert your best efforts to bring this about. i should like to mention another issue that constantly arises – quite rightly – in these negotiations, concerning investment in services and a service-based infrastructure of developing countries. liberalisation in services is as important a part of the inbuilt agenda of this round as agriculture. i want to stress that our purpose in these negotiations is to boost commerce, because trade drives inter-economic growth. but boosting commerce, to my mind, is not the same as commercialising what other countries and governments legitimately want to keep within the public realm. that is their choice. that is the policy space to which they are entitled. no part of this negotiation concerning the liberalisation of services seeks to erode, let alone remove, the right to regulate public services. take the example of water, as one member already mentioned: where are developing countries going to get the capital investment, the transfer of technology, the transfer of management skills to operate the most efficient water industry in their countries that they can possibly get, to bring about the distribution that they so desperately need, if it is without foreign investment, foreign know-how and foreign transfer of technology? we must keep a sense of perspective about this whilst recognising and safeguarding developing countries’ rights to regulation. with regard to agriculture – and incidentally, there is no question of excluding agriculture from these negotiations; anyone who ever dreamed that might be either desirable or possible has long since seen that dream disappear, never to return – we have an obligation to liberalise trade in agriculture, but we have to do it in a way and at a pace that are manageable and absorbable by european farm communities and that strike the right balance between the interests of different sorts of developing country; and, as i say, they are not the same. however, as european agriculture changes and evolves, the importance of specialised production and products and of those products associated with geographical indications becomes ever greater. that is why the protection of gis remains not only an important but also an indispensable condition for our completion of this round. i say this not only to mrs mann but also to others. this is a single undertaking and that means that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. in my view that is very important. it is a necessary protection that each wto member has to ensure that their vital interests are not shunned or overlooked. if there were no single undertaking, no principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, then we would be much weakened and not only us but also other wto members would be less able to protect their vital interests. in my view gis are of vital interest. in conclusion – and i am very much aware that i have not responded to many of the points made or taken up a number of the points – nama is an important issue; i shall address these other issues in remarks i shall be making in a week’s time – let me just say that these multilateral trade talks are very important. why? because multilateralism is important. multilateral processes and institutions are important. yes, the european union will pay extra into this round and into this system in order to keep alive, to strengthen and to carry forward the multilateral values and principles that are at the heart of this round. we will not pay indefinitely and we are not a bottomless pit, but it is true that we are prepared to pay for our principles, not only for the sake of our principles, but also because in a multilateral trade round the potential benefits for the global economy and for us in europe and for the poor and needy people around the world are multiplied to a far greater extent through a multilateralisation of the agreement that we reach than any set of bilateral agreements between ourselves and other countries or regions could possibly achieve. i am not ignoring the bilateral agenda. indeed, we have negotiations, whether it be ongoing, in the case of the gulf states; asean, potentially, when we have our roadmap put in place; and mercosur. incidentally, we need to consider what we are going to keep back from this multilateral agreement for our bilateral mercosur negotiation. first and foremost we must make the multilateral talks successful. it will be a huge challenge in the coming months to achieve that, the way in which we can strengthen international trade rules to drive up standards of trade and social and labour rights, and trade in environment as well. there is a very great deal to achieve in a relatively short space of time. if in the coming months i can get as much negotiation in as mrs kinnock did in her one-and-a-half minutes, i will be travelling at a reasonable rate. it is a wee bit challenging for me to do that. however, given the number of things you have mentioned and registered, which we will carry on in our discussion tomorrow morning, if i can match a part of the same rate of progress i will not be doing badly. as can be seen from the speeches which have already been made here, this proposal for a directive has generated a huge controversy which extends significantly beyond this house and involves many port operators as well as the general public working in the sector. i would like to stress that we understand their protest but we do not accept the violence with which they have done so. the two committees of this parliament which were called upon to give an opinion on the proposal for a directive both decided to reject it, further undermining its political destiny. the importance of the port sector, mr president, need not be stressed or demonstrated. we all know that almost all external trade in the european union is carried out through its ports and that the workforce associated with port traffic amounts to 350 000 direct jobs, to which we must of course add the indirect jobs. on the other hand, cargo handling techniques and equipment are constantly evolving, which requires continuous investment and renewal. the questions that arise are therefore as follows: is the proposed directive beneficial or not for investment, competition and market access? does it respect the rights acquired in respect of existing operators or not? does it violate the principle of subsidiarity or not? is it fair or unfair as regards compensation in the event of substitution of providers? does it affect the labour market and the social rights of workers in the sector? in short, is it achieving or not achieving the objectives it has set itself of greater efficiency, better competition, more internal market and better services? it is to these questions that the rapporteur, mr jarzembowski, has sought to respond with a great sense of balance, and for this i wish to congratulate him. but it seems to me that this proposal for a directive, even in the circumstances in which it was presented by the commission, needs to be revised in the context of a genuine political strategy to stimulate the development of european ports, as the rapporteur himself points out and amends, and which takes account of the current market situation and involves the cooperation of all the parties concerned, including of course the european parliament. the commissioner has the answer. it is obvious that this will make it much easier for us to take a decision consistent with the objectives we have set out.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we all agree that the sugar reform is necessary to make this sector more sustainable, in line with the latest reform of the cap, and consistent with the european union's international obligations. however, and despite these new objectives, the reform as proposed by the commission raises serious problems for european farmers, in particular by the excessive reduction in the price of sugar. i therefore support mr fruteau's report and the work of the various political groups in the committee on agriculture, which i believe sends a very clear message to the commission and the council. in addition to limiting the price reduction to 30% in the sugar cmo, amendment no 3 also strengthens the farmers' support system, i.e. the possibility for reform. however, i must say that unfortunately the commission's proposal was drawn up more from the perspective of the processing industry than that of agricultural producers and more in the interests in writing. we abstained from the final vote on the resolution on the financial perspective (2007-2013) because we did not agree with the wording of paragraph 4 of the resolution. we believe that the minimum agreement reached was a good agreement for europe, because it allowed the serious political crisis threatening the european union to be averted, even if only temporarily. the use of the word 'rejected' in paragraph 4 conveys to the european public the idea that the european parliament intends to resume the financial debate, which in the present situation will not be possible, let alone desirable. we therefore understand the term 'rejected' as equivalent to 'disaccord', which obviously does not call into question the agreement already reached.
in writing. in december, the council ignored the ep's right/obligation to co-decide and forgot to finance policies central to the lisbon strategy and to europe's action in the world. as a result, the commission is left without resources for citizenship policies, in particular for youth, education, research and culture, to finance the globalisation adjustment fund and for commitments under the union's external action, including peacekeeping missions and countering the proliferation of wmd. i therefore voted in favour of rejecting the agreement in its present form, calling for the opening of a negotiating process to find the missing resources. the presidency should be mandated to negotiate with the ep flexibility reserves to ensure all the necessary resources and to agree a review clause to allow for a review of expenditure in 2008, including the diversion of cap funding to competitiveness and innovation policies, and to reconsider the union's own budgetary resources. it is not a question of reopening the agreement reached in brussels in december, but of supplementing it with the necessary means to finance policies and actions which are indispensable for a more cohesive and competitive europe and a more responsible and credible europe as a global actor.
in writing. the agreement on the community budget for 2007-13, adopted at the december european council, is grossly inadequate in terms of financial resources and inadequate in its priorities and instruments to respond to the economic, social and environmental needs and problems of an enlarged eu of 27 countries. the so-called 'solidarity' is under-represented, with the weight of cohesion policy funding falling from 0.41% of community gni to just 0.37%, despite the increase in economic and social disparities resulting from enlargement. cuts are also made in the social, environmental, agricultural, cooperation, research and cultural fields, while at the same time 'competitiveness', migration control, border and security policies and the common foreign and security policy are financially strengthened, to the detriment of development aid. the interests of the economically more developed countries and their large economic and financial groups have thus triumphed over the interests of the so-called 'cohesion' countries, such as portugal, and of the workers. the whole 'negotiation' process was characterised by the submission of successive proposals, each one more negative than the previous one. the resolution also rejects the council's agreement but reaffirms the ep's negotiating position, which is already inadequate in terms of finances and priorities.
in writing. in the text adopted on the financial perspective, there are two points which would deserve a different treatment. the first is the wording by which the agreement reached in the european council is 'rejected'. there are other terms more appropriate to express the non-acceptance of this agreement. the second is the way in which agricultural policy is mentioned. the way in which some european states have received the most significant funds from the union budget through the cap has made it difficult to advance the process of european integration, preventing more appropriate criteria for allocating funds. for portugal, the agreement reached in the council is positive. but the european parliament has every right to want to initiate a process leading to its improvement. in this process, there was no significant shift in the budgetary methodology and the overall allocation criteria for funds were not changed. solidarity with the southern and eastern cohesion states must continue to be guaranteed. it is essential that support for increased european competitiveness does not disadvantage the currently less competitive economies.
in writing. the first of all duties of a co-decision maker is a sense of responsibility. as has been publicly and notoriously noted, the process leading to the adoption of the financial perspective last december was a complex one, which has revealed how difficult these negotiations can be, particularly in the circumstances in which they are taking place today. i believe, as i have already had the opportunity to say, that the final result of the december summit, although it is less than i would have liked and advocated, is a positive result overall and in the interests of europe and portugal. i therefore think it is legitimate to try to improve this agreement, but never at the risk of losing the consensus we have reached. the interests at stake are too important for the main concern to be primarily in the context of institutional balance.
in writing. i voted against the european council's agreement on the financial perspective because i consider it symptomatic of the crisis europe is going through: it's poor, it's unambitious and it's not inspiring. it is poor in financial amounts when compared to the other institutional partners. but it is also poor because the european council's proposal is more a summation of the demands put forward by the different member states than an expression of any kind of political will. it has no ambition to show any obvious signs of inconsistency with previously adopted policies. the frustration of european citizens and their sense of ineffectiveness towards the european institutions is heightened when decisions are taken one day and presented to public opinion as clear signs of progress on certain matters of interest to europeans, and then the next day the council itself does not guarantee in the financial perspective the means for these actions to go ahead. finally, this agreement does not generate any enthusiasm because it does not honour the commitments made to the applicant countries (bulgaria and romania). this kind of attitude is called hypocrisy in english.
in writing. the europe of freedom and values must clearly and transparently assert the unequivocal protection of citizens' rights and the primacy of the law in the rule of law. the fight against terrorism must be done in this field. in this way, not only do we not betray our cultural heritage, but we also enjoy broad international support and we are distinguished from terrorists by our profound respect for people and all their rights. this temporary committee should develop its work in order to collect and analyse all information that is relevant to ascertaining the veracity of the facts reported by the washington post and corroborated by human rights watch. it is essential that the truth be revealed, not only because persistent doubt ends up feeding suspicion and encouraging speculation, but also because it is clear that under no circumstances can we allow european territory to be used for secret detention practices, as this would be shameful and would be clearly in conflict with international human rights rules and with european rules and values themselves.
in writing. conflict situations, particularly the military conflict in which the united states and its allies are involved, require even greater attention to respect for the fundamental values, the civilization values, which we defend. it's in extreme situations that you have to be more demanding. i therefore support all those in europe and the united states who have raised their voices against any abuse or disregard of these values. in that sense, i stand here, as i have had occasion to do on other occasions, and express my clear position. that said, and with regard to the so-called 'cia flights', i cannot but deplore the terms in which this debate has been conducted, a debate often based on allegations, suspicions and vague accusations where the word of our allies and the highest political leaders of the member states seems to be the least valued. in this context, i believe that the conference of presidents has succeeded in finding a justified solution, which is above all balanced and compatible with the role which the european parliament can play in this matter, and that is why i voted in favour of it.
in writing. our commitment to what should be, in a broad sense, the whole middle east peace process requires that the european union take a clear and consistent stand in defence of democracy, the rule of law and human rights. in this case, the steps taken in lebanon require our support not only in form but also in substance and in practice, which means, in particular, our cooperation in all matters relating to the search for the truth in the case of the assassination of former prime minister rafiq hariri. i therefore voted in favour of this report, but i do not want to leave out the procedural issues raised by the rapporteur, which i think deserve attention.
in writing. the final report of the conciliation on the management of waste from the extractive industries, which is also of interest to portugal, was approved positively. with this new legislation, there is a strengthening of environmental rules in several member states and a greater obligation for industries to repair sites after they have ceased their industrial activities, taking on their responsibilities in protecting the environment and public health. equally important is the inventory of existing situations to be made so that appropriate action can be taken. let us hope that there is a consensual practice for these purposes.
in writing. this directive is an important piece of environmental legislation. after the commendable work of the rapporteur and the entire parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee, i can only express my support for this report given the important measures envisaged to help reduce the negative effects on the environment and the risks to human health resulting from waste from the extractive industries. i therefore voted in favour of mr sjöstedt's report.
in writing. i am clearly in favour of this proposal, which is of particular importance for my country, portugal, which has a coastline that is almost half the length of the national border, rich in rivers and other waterways, with a people with bathing habits and an increasing number of water sports practitioners. this proposal represents a significant step forward in terms of protecting public health and the environment, since the proposed amendments bring clear improvements in the knowledge, control and quality of bathing waters. the text obtained in the conciliation committee fills in gaps and updates the regulation currently in force on bathing water quality. the degree of demand has increased in the case of new bacteriological parameters for water quality to be considered 'sufficient', the mandatory nature of information and the right of public participation and the standardisation of signage in all eu countries, which represents a significant reduction in health risks and contributes to the prevention of diseases and infections.
in writing. the most important part of the solution is to update the 1976 bathing water directive, which is outdated in the face of the development of scientific knowledge and health requirements. the rapporteur believes that the implementation of these amendments will reduce the risks for bathers from 12% to 7.5%. this means that the very difficult reconciliation of very divergent positions has ended with a satisfactory but insufficient result, particularly as regards the parameters which are now mandatory. it is in the area of public information that there are the greatest gains. it is expected that the information will be made public in due course and visible at bathing water sites.
in writing. the text obtained in the conciliation committee and now being put to the vote contains very positive amendments to the proposal submitted at second reading on 21 april 2005. the non-incorporation of the proposal for the abolition of the distinction between coastal and inland waters in the package of measures to be adopted and the non-abolition in the final text of the classification of 'sufficient' quality safeguards portugal's best interests in this area and is in line with the latest recommendations of the who. i welcome the proposed parameters for assessing the quality of bathing water and the methodology adopted for their assessment and classification, and therefore support their adoption. i believe that this will not only improve the quality of the environment but also help to protect and inform citizens better about the quality of the bathing water they use.
in writing. the agreement reached in conciliation on the bathing water quality management directive is based on new criteria for water quality assessment and public information. for portugal, these criteria of greater demand and better information to the public are fundamental, not only because of the extent of the portuguese coast but also because of the social, cultural and economic value that this coast and its numerous waterways represent for the country, in terms of tourist activities but also in terms of socio-cultural activities. all measures must be taken to prevent and reduce health risks. i therefore consider this proposal to be of significant importance for the protection of public health and the environment. the proposed amendments therefore bring clear improvements in the knowledge, control and quality of bathing water, while maintaining the desired balance in terms of the costs associated with the introduction of the new quality criteria. i voted in favour of mr maaten's report.
in writing. we consider important the amendments adopted today to the report on the application of the provisions of the aarhus convention in the european institutions, which gives priority to the public's right to know the procedures for participation in decision-making, namely how to use them, the right of access to information and finally access to justice in environmental matters. for example, changes were made to the setting of environmental policy priorities and public participation in environmental policy-making, and it became mandatory to clearly indicate how to obtain information, including information on the status of infringement proceedings and the availability of information by considering the results of the various consultations. however, in some areas it falls short of the requirements of the convention, in particular in the area of access to justice, in that no assistance mechanisms are established to reduce or eliminate recurrent financial obstacles, and in the vast majority of cases access to justice is conditioned precisely by the lack of financial means of those who have recourse to it. but taken as a whole, it is an important step towards ensuring effective participation (through procedures developed within reasonable time limits) and access to information that allows for duly reasoned and democratic participation.
in writing. the european union can only develop and assert itself if it is based on values such as solidarity, peace, social coexistence and the uncompromising defence of public tranquillity. the debate in the european parliament on the directive on access to the market in port services took place in an environment of unlawful pressure and violence which resulted in unjustified material and personal damage. it is not acceptable to grant any benefits to those who break the law and the rules of coexistence. so, regardless of the intrinsic value of the matters dealt with in the directive and the balance of social interests achieved, i have decided to abstain.
, in writing. we voted against the proposal for a directive because we believe that a disorderly and uncontrolled liberalisation of access to the public services market will create serious problems for public safety and health, for the guarantee of the provision and sustainability of a service, also of a public nature, and will lead to a reduction in the effectiveness of the service itself. three years after the first commission proposal in this area, which was rejected at the time, we are again faced with a motion for a resolution voted against by the competent commission, a vote which sends a clear message to this parliament: a text which is likely to create a whole series of legal inconsistencies with the existing international regulatory framework but also with existing community law - for example, with regulation (eec) no 1191/69 on the obligations inherent in the concept of public service - and which favours a total deregulation of self-service cannot be considered positive. however, the same message goes further and clearly states that a proposal applicable to substantially different ports, where forced liberalization could generate economically negative monopolies and, finally, a proposal with harmful social consequences, cannot be considered on its merits as a proposal plausible for adoption by the representatives of the peoples of europe.
in writing. the proposal we tabled to reject the port services directive has been adopted! for the second time, the attempt to liberalize port services was defeated, following the significant mobilization of workers in the sector, who from the outset fought - strengthening and deepening existing contradictions - against this new offensive that attacked employment with rights and put a strategic sector for national development in the hands of the large international shipowners. but we must remain alert to any new attempt at the level of the european union to re-introduce what has now been rejected for the second time. we must firmly oppose any further attempts to liberalize port services, whether by including this sector in the unacceptable proposal for a directive on the internal market in services or by implementing it in stages by re-introducing the proposal for intra-community maritime traffic. as the workers point out, there is no justification for a community directive on the sector. at this moment we must welcome the victory of the workers' struggle in the port sector, a victory which is part of the struggle of workers in the various countries against the neo-liberal policies of the european union which, in pursuit of the interests of the large economic and financial groups, attack the rights of workers and the national public sector and services.
in writing. this declaration of vote is needed to accompany the european parliament in its satisfaction with the essential progress made in the democratization process in afghanistan over the past few years. the taliban regime is long gone, its horrors, its violation of the most elementary rules and principles of respect for human rights. not everything is done, but afghanistan today is, arguably, a better place than it had been in the past decades. this satisfaction cannot, however, ignore two aspects. on the one hand, as has already been said, there is still a lot to be done at various levels in afghanistan. on the other hand, the need for the international community, in particular the european union and its member states, to continue its committed aid, both in material and human terms, aware that this process is time-consuming but, as it turns out, encouraging.
in writing. the concern expressed by this motion for a resolution, as well as by others which have already been discussed in this parliament, deserves my agreement in all that concerns the enunciation of a set of principles which i stand by and defend. all hatred deserves our rejection, all discrimination before the law must be fought. there is, however, a set of explicit proposals in this resolution which i believe go beyond what i believe should be the scope of the european parliament and which i believe clearly invade what should be the sphere of the national states. in addition, there is a tendency among some political groups, which i do not share and which i reject, to try to get approval in the institutions of the european union for what is rejected in its member states. i disagree with that path. finally, i would remind you that phobias, as an expression of behavioural disorders, are not combated at the legislative or parliamentary level.
in writing. we are against all discrimination and violence. there can be no exception in this respect, no doubt or hesitation. but it is not to be confused with 'homophobia' to have a free democratic debate in the member states on their civil law, particularly on family law or personal status. that would create a framework of intellectual coercion and conditioning that is totally incompatible with an open and democratic society. you can't confuse disagreements with phobias. you cannot nurture or invent feelings of hatred and intolerance. to label disagreements as "phobias" is itself an extreme. much of the resolution does not, in fact, fit the definition of 'homophobia' set out in recital a, and thus loses its relevance and its relevance. in addition, in several respects it conflicts with the principle of subsidiarity, a guiding principle and foundation of the whole union, which only serves to harm the european construction. that is why i voted against it.
in writing. we consider the resolution tabled following the 11th conference of the parties to the montreal convention on climate change to be generally positive, as it underlines the willingness of the parties to comply with the kyoto protocol and deplores the us administration's reluctance to join any meaningful international partnership on climate change. however, we disagree with some points in the final resolution and regret that our proposals were not adopted. we particularly regret that the proposal which we support and which called for an urgent review of the relevant flexible mechanisms before the community's emissions trading scheme could be extended to other areas (e.g. aviation) was not voted on. we believe that an analysis is needed to demonstrate that such enlargement will contribute to combating climate change and that rich countries/areas will not be privileged at the expense of developing countries and industries. we also disagree with the insistence, even for the purpose of an evaluation, on the trading of pollution rights.
in writing. we voted in favour of the report which seeks to assess the environmental aspects of sustainable development and which makes some criticisms of the commission's position on the inadequacy of some guidelines and the scarcity of financial resources. although it does not clearly call into question the policies at the root of environmental problems, in particular the focus on competitiveness to the detriment of people and the environment, always subordinated to the logic of profit, it has positive aspects in its defence of less polluting transport, the role of land and forest planning, the need to ensure food supply. the relationship between poverty and the environment is also positive, although it is regrettable that the most important point in this area was rejected in plenary, including the assertion that the policies of liberalization do not address the problems of poverty and social exclusion and the criticism that the proposals on the fight against poverty, social exclusion and the increase in inequalities are inadequate.
in writing. today, sustainable development is without a shadow of a doubt a fundamental objective of the european union and a global challenge. sustainable development strategies therefore require a long-term political vision at the highest level. in the face of the social, environmental and democratic challenges we face, it is essential to act responsibly, not only at the level of public authorities, but also at the level of citizens. we must, however, be careful in all the measures we take with regard to our objectives of growth and social and economic development, which are fundamental for the future of our societies. this report not only assessed progress made since 2001, but also outlined new measures. in this process we must therefore reiterate the need to reaffirm sustainable development as a priority for the future of europe, while maintaining our objective of meeting the objectives of the lisbon strategy. i therefore voted in favour of mrs ferreira's report.

mr president, the european parliament is giving the go-ahead to a great debate today. political institutions and social actors, with the mobilization of the media, will take responsibility for facing the question: does europe want to win the future or not? the constitutional question is not simply a question of the architecture of institutions. it is above all the way in which europe combines the efficiency of its institutions with a moral conscience about the world. all of us, european citizens, in the corridors of power and in the union's vital space, feel this challenge. how to govern a vast, open cosmopolitan space? how can we achieve a project of justice that is both within and outside the borders of europe? how do you build a way of life that's not based on tradition? how can europe be made a democratic power, the founder of a new world order? how can we set an example for a union of peoples? how can we find a common form of defence of human rights in the world? how do you find a common way to influence the world? how do we give politics its programming power back over a globalised and deregulated economy? how do you connect fairness and efficiency? how to open the door to new political models? the future leaves us no room for fear. it is urgent to discuss political integration, to discuss a more cosmopolitan and humane way of life, to discuss the extent to which a constitution represents and builds our european identity, because our european identity is not born of tradition, our identity is born of morality, will and reason.

mr president, i welcome mr tannock's report on the new european neighbourhood policy, which should be one of the european union's most strategically important instruments, including from the point of view of global security, as commissioner ferrero-waldner has stressed, and which i also support. it is no good for the union to close itself off at its borders as a fortress to protect itself against terrorism, organised crime, drug trafficking, illegal immigration, trafficking in women and children, among other causes of insecurity. no matter how high the walls are, they'll always be permeable. lampedusa, ceuta and melilla are dramatic examples. good neighbourliness means increased security for neighbours. this is why it is important to implement this new policy properly, which will enable us to support our neighbours through specific programmes which have a direct impact on strengthening their security and ours. by helping them to solve their security problems we also contribute to widening the space of stability around us. but the european security ring that this new policy aims to build would present a gap on the south-western flank if cape verde, despite its strong links to europe and a common border with the european union through the canary islands, were not also a beneficiary of this instrument. the report must provide a solution that will enable this country to qualify for programmes under the european neighbourhood policy. the european union cannot allow cape verde to become the weakest link in its circle of neighbours. cape verde can and should play an important role in european and global security if it can benefit from programmes under the european neighbourhood policy. it is necessary to help the cape verdean authorities to prevent their territory from becoming a platform for organised crime, illegal immigration and terrorism. i therefore propose, with the support of my group, two amendments to the report, which i hope will have the general support of this parliament.
the neighbourhood policy must be a more open concept, not restricted to the mediterranean itself or to the eastern border of the european union. we must not forget that we have other neighbours on our atlantic sea borders. both because of their importance and because of the particular sensitivity they represent for european security, they should also deserve special attention in this context. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. some say that the cape verdean case has its own framework in the acp area. but that is too square and out of touch with reality. we must be able to define policies that make a fruitful, agile and imaginative cross-section of neighbourhood policy with other frameworks, whether in the acp or other fields. this is our need; and cape verde also deserves it for the exemplary performance of its people in democracy, good governance and respect for human rights, as well as the deep historical, social, political, cultural and geographical affinities with the european union. i therefore call for a vote in favour of amendments nos 11, 12, 36 and 38.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, as we have pointed out on several occasions, the reality confirms that the implementation of the lisbon strategy has given priority only to liberalization and labour flexibility, which, together with the stability pact, is having negative repercussions in the social field, affecting women in particular. it is not enough to proclaim the need for urgent action to promote employment, quality of employment and social inclusion of women in order to achieve the lisbon objectives. the policies that are undermining equal rights and perpetuating discrimination against women, particularly in the labour market, must be changed. in addition to the increase in unemployment among thousands of women affected by the restructuring and relocation of multinationals and by the industrial sectors affected by the liberalization of international trade, such as textiles, clothing, footwear and many others, the new jobs created are increasingly precarious, poorly paid, discriminatory and disrespectful of the rights of working women. however, within the framework of the so-called 'lisbon strategy', new proposals for directives are under discussion which could further aggravate discrimination against women, contributing to the worsening of unemployment and social exclusion. the cases of the proposed directive on the organization of working time and the infamous bolkenstein directive on liberalization in the services sector are noteworthy. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens is a very good one. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption.
in writing. a code of discipline on members must be designed with the greatest parsimony. the subject is controversial. parliament is freedom made institution. it was in political representation that democracy found the ideal way to fulfil its legitimating foundation - legislation as an act of the will of those represented, as consent, as autonomy. and this is how democratic political systems have characterised the parliamentary institution: publicity and transparency of debates, popular control of members in periodic elections. representatives have the "special status" that comes with being the "map of the people". your freedom is a right and a duty. your responsibility is political. your trial is, as popper said, election day. that is why the epp has taken a very cautious approach in the committee on constitutional affairs. because a code like this has limits. the limits that come from the integrity of the exercise of the mandate. the limits of the freedom with which the people made parliament, in which they represent themselves in parliament and which they do not want to see amputated in parliament.
in writing. the sense of responsibility, respect and intellectual elevation with which the mandate of a member of parliament must be exercised have never been incompatible with the ways in which members express themselves. on the contrary, i did. while it is true that some intolerable excesses are well known, it is equally true that some countries even cultivate practices and customs which in no way diminish the prestige of their assemblies, even giving them a character of their own and idiosyncratic. consider, for example, the british case. i therefore believe that it is mainly practice - which in the case of the european parliament is necessarily still in the making - that will determine rules and behaviour - in addition, of course, to what is laid down in the regulations in force. the mandate of a member of the european parliament is an exercise of freedom and responsibility and there is no reason to believe that the elected representatives lack either of these.
