in writing. the report on the european charter for small enterprises is of great importance given the nature of the european business fabric, which is mainly composed of small enterprises. as rapporteur on sustainable tourism for the union, i cannot help but follow the measures being taken in this key area for tourism, which is without doubt the most promising economic sector for european economic growth and development. we note that the training of the workforce, the development of the entrepreneurial spirit and the improvement of legislation are the priorities which will make it possible to exploit the strengths of this sector, to combat its weaknesses and to support growth in the various countries which have signed the charter. i therefore voted in favour of mrs vlasto's report.
in writing. smes are the backbone of the european economy, job creation and regional development. the involvement of smes is therefore fundamental and unavoidable for the achievement of the objectives of the lisbon strategy, which aim to strengthen sustainable growth and the creation of more and better jobs. i therefore support the implementation of a european sme charter by enabling eu member states to benefit from their respective experiences through the exchange of good practice. this implementation report aims to strengthen the sme dimension in community policies and therefore recommends the rationalisation of existing european instruments. this report also draws attention once again to the difficulties faced by smes in accessing community programmes and their funding. in addition to these obstacles to access, the situation will tend to worsen as the financial envelope for the next financial perspective (2007-2013), as approved by the european council, has been the victim of blind cuts of the order of 50% of the funds. these include projects benefiting smes under the 'competitiveness, growth and jobs' category and, more specifically, the 7th framework programme for development and the competitiveness and innovation programme.
in writing. i recognize the need to reform the european sugar sector. however, in order to be fair and effective, the reform must strike a balance between:the international trade commitments undertaken;the proposed objectives of increasing the competitiveness of the sector;the stability of the community market;the viability and sustainability of the sector, in particular with regard to guaranteeing the incomes of european producers; and the preferential trade regime granted by the european union to acp countries and least developed countries, notably through incentives for sugar exports to the eu under the 'everything but arms' initiative. to this end, the broad guidelines for the reform proposed in this report, as well as the amendments to this effect to improve the european commission's reform proposals, concerning: a more moderate price reduction; the establishment of trade regulations; the implementation of measures to mitigate the economic impact of the reform; and support for the development of alternative products for the disposal of sugar production, seem appropriate to me and deserve my agreement. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. it is agreed that reform of the sugar sector is necessary to make this important sector more sustainable in line with the latest cap reform and consistent with the eu's international obligations. however, and despite these noble aims, the reform as proposed by the commission raises serious problems for european farmers, in particular the excessive reduction in the price of sugar. i therefore support mr fruteau's reports and the outcome of the work of the various political groups in the committee on agriculture, which i believe send a very clear message to the commission and the council. in addition to the limitation of the price reduction to 30% in the sugar cmo, i would stress amendment no 3, namely the possibility for member states to continue to be able to benefit from a certain amount of production-related subsidies, thus avoiding the rapid extinction of the sugar sector in the european regions most vulnerable to this reform. i would also stress the safeguarding of the possibility for the restructuring fund to support those who renounce only part of their quota (amendment no 7), thus allowing some industries to be helped in their conversion.
in writing. the sugar reform is necessary to make this sector more sustainable, following the latest cap reform. however, this reform could cause serious problems for european farmers, in particular by excessively reducing the price of sugar. the fact that the commission's proposal was drawn up more in the interests of the large surplus producing countries than in the interests of the small ones, such as portugal, which do not even have beet production to supply their consumption, only reminds us that it is not countries like portugal that are distorting the international market. i would like to recall the possibility, proposed in this report, that member states may continue to benefit from a certain amount of subsidies linked to production, thus avoiding the rapid extinction of the sugar sector in the regions most vulnerable to this reform. it seems to me that the possibility of the restructuring fund and the support for those who renounce only part of their quota have been safeguarded, so that some industries, such as the portuguese, can be reoriented away from agriculture to support the processing side. i therefore voted in favour of mr fruteau's reports.
in writing. the report in question deserves my support, and i have therefore voted in favour of it. the european constitution is not dead! the 'no' vote in the french and dutch referendums on the treaty establishing a constitution for europe did not mean its 'death', but only the suspension of its ratification, which was then under way. however, in view of the negative result of the french and dutch referendums, it does not seem possible to continue trying to ratify the current text without amending it. however, it is out of the question to abandon the draft constitution altogether. a constitutional agreement, as the rapporteurs point out, is indispensable for the european union to (re) gain the trust of european citizens, to maintain the momentum of european integration and to assert a credible role on the international scene. in this sense, the 'period of reflection' should serve to relaunch the draft constitution on the basis of a broad public debate on the future of europe involving citizens, civil society, the social partners and national and regional parliaments. this debate should seek to clarify, deepen and improve the european constitution, to examine the criticisms which have been levelled at it and to find solutions to the constitutional crisis, as well as to respond to the aspirations of european citizens.
in writing. we voted against this report because we consider it to be an unacceptable pressure on the member states and their democratic institutions, after the people of france and the netherlands rejected the european constitution. although the european parliament recognises that ratification of the constitution now faces 'difficulties which may prove insurmountable' unless action can be taken to respond to the concerns expressed in france, the netherlands and other member states, a majority insists that the current reflection period be transformed into a relaunch of the constitutional project, on the basis of a broad public debate on the future of european integration. what the majority of the ep wants is a major propaganda campaign to put pressure on the people to accept the so-called european constitution. while we agree that the treaty of nice does not constitute a basis for future prospects - which is why we voted against it - we are opposed to attempts to pursue a path of deepening neoliberalism, federalism and militarism. we want a europe where there is greater cooperation between sovereign and equal states, greater economic and social cohesion, more solidarity and a europe which is truly committed to peace and social progress.
in writing. the majority of meps - including the ps/psd - approved a report which, as the popular saying goes, 'makes the party, launches the rockets and catches the canes'. under the guise of a 'period of reflection', he says a debate is needed, but for which - let the devil take them - he has already drawn his conclusion: 'relaunch the constitutional project'; 'avoid another setback'; 'deepen' the 'consensus on the european constitution'; 'publicity', with 'appropriate funding', to 'reassure and convince public opinion'; 'ensure that it comes into force', 'during 2009'. the ep is not only not competent in this area, but it is also trying to hide the fact that the so-called 'european constitution' has not already been rejected, which is not true. it was rejected by the french and dutch peoples and has since ceased to have any value, as provided for in the treaties. it is no coincidence that the european union's largest employer (unice) states in the terms of reference it has submitted to the austrian presidency that 'there is an urgent need to find a way out of the eu's institutional crisis'. and criticism: the "pause for reflection..., seems to be more pause than reflection". the big business in europe and the political forces that implement its guidelines, once again disregarding the expressed will of the people, are trying to take the initiative.
in writing. i congratulate mr duff and mr voggenhuber on the excellent report they have produced on the reflection period: structure, themes and context for an assessment of the debate on european union - and i agree with the proposal that this reflection period should be used to relaunch the constitutional project on the basis of a broad public debate on the future of european integration. i also agree with the suggestion that this new democratic dialogue, which should be seen as an opportunity to promote democracy in europe, should be conducted and coordinated throughout the union, structured around common themes and in realistic phases, according to an agreed evaluation framework and designed to lead to decisive policy choices. i recognise the strategic importance of political institutions in encouraging a proactive attitude of the media, in particular the local television, press and radio, by mobilising them for publicity and intensifying the debate. i also agree that the conclusions of the reflection period should be drawn up by the second half of 2007 at the latest, and that a clear decision should then be taken on how to proceed with the european constitution, and that in any event every effort should be made to ensure that the european constitution enters into force during 2009.
in writing. the need to adapt the institutional structure of the european union to its immediate future, bearing in mind its possible enlargements, is present in our concerns. i agree with the idea that we will have to resume the institutional debate shortly. i also believe that the debate on the 'constitutional treaty' must be concluded. the idea that there should be reflection and debate on this matter and that there should be a definitive moment deserves my agreement and will have my support. however, the idea, implicit in the thinking of some, that only one outcome is possible, whatever it may be, that one has not my agreement, nor will it have my support. the debate, and in particular the debate which citizens are asked to have, is by its nature open and free, and any attempt to condition it will merit my active objection.
in writing. the eu cannot relegate to the background its duty as a great defender of respect for international law and the development of a social market economy. to do this we need to shape the eu's face in the world, giving the european neighbourhood policy (enp) an absolutely pivotal role in maintaining constructive relations with those closest to us, with a view to building an area of peace and prosperity. my vote in favour of the tannock report is based on the importance it attaches to the values enshrined in article 6 of the maastricht treaty as the cornerstone of the enp, while making it clear that this policy is not an alternative to eu membership. finally, i welcome the recognition of the contribution that future partners, such as cape verde, will bring to our joint fight against terrorism, the illegal arms trade, poverty and human slavery. this recognition is due to their excellent geostrategic position and the fundamental reforms that many of them have carried out, while not forgetting a long-standing cultural and historical affinity resulting from their close geographical proximity to both the european continent and the outermost regions, including those in the atlantic.
in writing. the european neighbourhood policy (enp) demonstrates the high priority the eu gives to building future relations with its neighbours, irrespective of possible accession. it is indeed in the eu's interest to contribute to democratic development in its immediate neighbourhood. the enp should more clearly develop a strategy for relations with neighbours that contributes to the construction and development of a common area of peace, stability, security, respect for human rights, democracy, the rule of law and prosperity, as well as offering third countries privileged relations and a leading position in the eu's external relations with other regions of the world. i support the rapporteur's proposals which stress the need to increase funding for the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument to deal with the problem of access to the single market, to define a clear strategy for the fight against international terrorism and organised crime, to improve links in energy and transport networks and to cooperate in the field of the environment. finally, special attention should be paid to energy policy, as the eu is surrounded by the world's largest oil and natural gas reserves.
in writing. the european union has the means and conditions to be a relevant player on the international scene. not in the way some would like, but not without being an important player in international relations. this reflection comes in the context of the european neighbourhood policy - understood both formally and in substance - since it is precisely here, in my view, that the union can and must play its main role at international level. i am in favour of further enlargement, but i am aware that this process is finite and that it will always be necessary to develop policies to promote a vast area of peace, security and prosperity around our area. this is both a geostrategic necessity and a moral obligation. i therefore consider it of the utmost importance that parliament should closely monitor this policy - and its financial framework - because it is here that it is possible to move from the proclamatory to the effective level. the example of the mediterranean experience is not one to leave us reassured or hopeful. others are, though. let us, then, follow our own good examples.
in writing. cape verde demonstrates exemplary performance in democracy, good governance and respect for human rights and has deep historical, social, political, cultural and geographical affinities with the european union. these make it a privileged and exceptional platform for the development and strengthening of the euro-african relationship and a factor of stability and security on one of the flanks of the european space. despite being europe's south-western atlantic frontier, cape verde has been included in other programmes which, by themselves, do not reflect its true proximity, nor do they recognise its identification with common values such as the rule of law, the promotion of good neighbourly relations and the principles of market economy and sustainable development. it is known that contacts have been developed between the cape verdean authorities and the main opposition party to promote the granting of special status or partnership with the european union. the inclusion of this country in the neighbourhood policy could be an important step in this direction and a decisive counterpoint to a neighbourhood policy which would be very poor if it were strictly centred on the southern and eastern borders of the union. i welcome the adoption of amendments nos 36 and 38.
in writing. the economic, social and environmental renewal of the european union envisaged in the lisbon strategy aims to promote a more dynamic and competitive europe of knowledge, accompanied by a qualitative and quantitative improvement in employment and greater social cohesion. i subscribe substantially to these objectives, but my concern goes above all to european families facing the persistent inequalities in our societies. these need to be countered in such a way as to promote a balance between work, family and private life. only then will we build a society based on education and lifelong learning, with knowledge and information for our citizens as its cornerstones. for these reasons, i voted in favour of the report by mrs edite estrela.
in writing. social inclusion and respect for gender equality are fundamental principles underpinning the lisbon strategy. however, these principles are still good intentions. the reality of gender equality is indeed confrontational: differences in employment rates, pay, access to and progression in the labour market, levels of education, participation in vocational training programmes, and greater difficulty in reconciling work and family life. although equal treatment is a fundamental principle of community law, it is urgent to move from political principles to concrete action. the diagnosis is long-standing. the catch is it's always the same: the member states lack the courage and determination to implement the solutions already identified. the financial perspective, as adopted by the european council, does not bode well, given the brutal cuts to the funds most closely linked to the lisbon strategy. i hope that the negotiations between the european parliament, the commission and the council will be able to minimise the damage already done.
the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, the high representative, in the introduction to his statement, pointed out that the first 31 days of this year and thus of the austrian presidency of the council were a turbulent period. indeed they were. the first council meeting, chaired by the austrian foreign minister two days ago, proved this by the agenda. it was important that we in the council had the opportunity to discuss the issues that mr solana raised in so many of his speeches and to take decisions with a clear statement. it is important that the european union should be closed to the outside world and be clear and unambiguous on the important issues of today's world. we are of course doing this together with the commission, and we are also seeking dialogue and discussion with you in the european parliament. i would remind you that during the 31 days of the austrian presidency the foreign minister, many other council presidents and i myself have had several opportunities to discuss with the european parliament many of the issues which interest you. i would also like to recall that i had the opportunity - and i am very grateful for that - yesterday in the committee on foreign affairs to report on the foreign policy aspects of the first council meeting under the austrian presidency. we want to continue to offer this willingness to talk as the austrian presidency of the council and to continue to talk to the european parliament. in this brief statement i would like to concentrate on two main points: firstly, the annual report from the council to the european parliament on the main aspects and basic options of the common foreign and security policy - our agenda item - and secondly, the relations between the european parliament and the council with regard to the cfsp budget. the first is that the council will draw up a report setting out the main aspects and basic options of the common foreign and security policy, including the financial implications for the general budget. this is provided for in the 1999 interinstitutional agreement on budgetary discipline and improvement of the budgetary procedure. the council accordingly submitted to the european parliament in april 2005 the report for 2004, which is on our agenda today. in this 2005 report, the council seeks to respond to parliament's request to reflect the european security strategy. the report therefore paid particular attention to the important issues of the security strategy. the following common foreign and security policy issues were discussed in particular: crisis management and conflict prevention, the fight against terrorism, disarmament and non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and small arms, external relations in different geographical regions, etc. the aim was to produce a comprehensive report covering the full range of results and activities in the field of the common foreign and security policy. these reports are in line with the reporting requirements and help to increase the visibility and transparency of work on cfsp matters. an effort has also been made to accommodate the views of the european parliament and therefore a special chapter has been included in the report, which contains the outlook for future activities and gives indications for activities in the coming year and for possible responses to emerging crises. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the development of the common foreign and security policy and the european security and defence policy is undoubtedly one of the success stories of the european union. crisis management operations in the balkans, africa, asia and the middle east have helped to raise the profile of the european union at international level. it is a priority to continue this path in line with the european security strategy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in the conclusions of the agreement on the next financial perspective, the european council 'calls on the budgetary authority to increase the budgetary appropriations for the common foreign and security policy for the period from 2007 onwards significantly in order to cover the actual foreseeable budgetary needs estimated on the basis of annual projections drawn up by the council, while still leaving a reasonable margin for unforeseen activities'. the agreement of the trilogue on an increase of the cfsp budget by 40 million for the current year 2006 to a total of 102.6 million is a step in the right direction. however, we have great challenges ahead of us. the european union's action in kosovo is likely to require substantial resources that cannot be covered by the current cfsp budget for 2006. work is under way to determine how to deal with such a situation. the presidency report on the esdp to the european council invited the austrian presidency to continue work to ensure adequate funding for civilian esdp missions from the cfsp budget. the presidency looks forward to working constructively with the european parliament on this issue. in line with the agreement reached at the trilogue on the 2006 budget, the presidency will shortly be providing the first information on this. the political and security committee's ambassador is expected to report on this in march this year. in conclusion, i would like to reiterate that the presidency looks forward to working constructively with the european parliament to achieve the objective of an increased and more efficient cfsp budget in the negotiations on the future interinstitutional agreement and in the 2007 budgetary procedure. (applause from the centre)
member of the commission. mr president, while in 2004 and 2005 we saw the terrible scenario of the tsunami, i agree with mr solana that this year, particular political challenges lie ahead. i would like to start with ukraine and russia, because that brings me to a very important point. as you know, the commission – president barroso, commissioner piebalgs and i – have been working both in the background and at the forefront in order to facilitate the dialogue between ukraine and russia. the important thing is, firstly, that we – as well as they – have come to a solution. secondly, we also have learned a very important lesson from this, namely that the question of energy is of great importance and has to be placed much higher on our political agenda. the issue of energy covers energy security, the question of diversification and the ways of dealing with this question in the future. the commission will therefore prepare a communication on this matter, which will take all these issues into account. the second point i would like to make concerns the palestinian elections. i wish to pay tribute to mrs de keyser. we met in gaza two weeks ago under difficult circumstances, when the security situation was still unclear. we thought that hamas would have 30-40% of the votes. like everybody else, we were taken by surprise. however, let me say that the most important thing is that the elections were held freely, fairly and in relative security. this is already an achievement. it leads me to believe that election observation missions are becoming more and more important. we see it in sri lanka, palestine, gaza and afghanistan, to name just a few. in the future, we will see it in congo and in haiti. this is a very important tool that we will certainly want to use in favour of all our european friends in parliament and council and in favour of the european public. to come back to palestine, we had a very important council meeting on monday and a quartet meeting on monday evening. mr solana has already reported on the main thrust of the three important principles: there has to be a commitment to non-violence, the new palestinian government has to recognise the state of israel, and it also has to stand by its existing obligations, i.e. oslo and the roadmap. however, we are also faced with a challenge. the caretaker government could stay in place for two to three months. what do we do, in particular with regard to financial support? we in the commission have to find solutions. i have already said that we would try to release eur 10 million from our infrastructure facility – there is some money there to be disbursed. we also said we would help with the utilities, paying these directly to the israelis in order to help that government too. however, we also have to see what can be done with the money in our world bank trust fund. it was blocked and has not been disbursed because the benchmarks had not yet been met. a world bank mission will be going there and we will have to see what can be done. this means that we will try to work in a coherent way, together with the president, the council, the council secretariat and mr solana to see which are the best instruments to use in order to make the foreign policy coherent, speedy and effective as quickly as possible. whilst on the subject of foreign policy issues, the ukrainian elections are forthcoming. within the last hour i met boris tarasyuk. we know how important these elections will be. again, an election observation team from the oecd, perhaps with your support, will be important. we could also say that a lot was done in 2005, for example, on the market economy status, where we were working with the ukrainians. we could work on quite a number of issues that are important, such as visa facilitation and readmission. we hope that after free and fair elections we can offer them an enhanced agreement, perhaps a free trade agreement. that would give them an even better stance and approach towards us. all of that brings me to the more general questions. both mr brok and mr winkler, the president-in-office, have stressed the importance of the coherence between the different instruments at the disposal of the european union under the first and second pillars. i could not agree more. in our view, it is a very important task to ensure that all eu foreign policy instruments – development aid, diplomacy, trade policy, civilian and military crisis management, institution-building, humanitarian assistance – work as part of a coherent whole, like interlinked cogs in a well-oiled machine. after all, this is the rationale behind the commission being ‘fully associated’ with common foreign and security policy. it also reflects the direction in which the constitutional treaty was taking us. as mr brok’s report highlights, the security challenges we face span the fields covered by all three eu pillars. security is not only about defence and military deployment, it is also about civilian crisis management and the wise management of bilateral relationships – and we have a lot of those. it is also about public health: think of avian flu. it is about the environment: think of the kyoto protocol. it is about the fight against terrorism and organised crime. yesterday we had the afghanistan conference. it is also about working together for institution-building, or fighting the scourge of drugs. we have so many instruments that we can use and apply together. it is not only about energy supplies and prices, but also about the fight against poverty in the world, and our ability to integrate our immigrant populations. the european union is increasingly called upon to face these global responsibilities in the field of peace and security. we now have an impressive toolbox with which to do so. but a smart toolbox is no good if the tools do not work very closely together. this, therefore, has to be our aim. an effective crisis response requires instruments that complement one another. we need strong community instruments working alongside the instruments of the cfsp. it is a recipe that can work. for example, our contribution to the aceh peace process is a mix of cfsp and community instruments. the commission also financed, for instance, president ahtisaari’s peace negotiations using the rapid reaction mechanism. we have therefore tried to be flexible. the cfsp launched the aceh monitoring mission to monitor compliance with the peace agreement. at the same time, for instance, the commission and member states, working with the international community, put in place a package of long-term measures to support the peace process. another example is the border assistance mission in moldova and ukraine, where the commission is funding the deployment of mobile teams to provide advice and on-the-job training to moldovan and ukrainian border and customs officials. the long-term objective of facilitating a resolution of the transnistria conflict matches that of the eu’s special representative. the border assistance mission and the eu special representative therefore work closely together. our head of mission also acts as his senior political adviser, and one of his team is based at our mission’s premises. early results are highly positive. community assistance enhances the impact of the cfsp assistance, and vice versa. in neither case would the european union’s contribution have been comprehensive or meaningful without utilising both community and cfsp instruments. and most importantly, its impact on the ground – on peoples’ lives – would be significantly reduced. we also need to enhance the eu’s existing instruments in support of our security objectives. diplomacy requires carrots and sticks, whether we are talking about weapons of mass destruction or promoting stability and prosperity in our neighbourhood. access to the world’s biggest internal market or our sizeable assistance programmes is a considerable carrot. this complementary use of community and cfsp instruments needs to become the rule, not the exception. in 2006 the task for us all – parliament, the council and the commission – is to work to improve the coherence of our different pillars and policies. the issue will also be dealt with in the concept paper on the eu’s external project which president barroso announced at hampton court, now planned for the june european council. the commission will focus in particular on building up its crisis response capacities. within dg external relations a ‘crisis platform’ will improve both internal and external policy coordination and will also ensure a more efficient implementation of projects and operations. it will complement our existing instruments such as the civil protection mechanism, humanitarian assistance and the rapid reaction mechanism. we also want to build on our strategy for disaster alert and preparedness. under the new financial perspectives, the stability instrument will also help ensure continuity between short- and long-term interventions. our aim is to develop flexible and responsive solutions to crisis situations and thus be a better partner for the military component of crisis response. finally, we will also cooperate very closely with the two arms of the budgetary authority to ensure adequate resources for cfsp. the commission welcomes the substantial increase of the cfsp budget in 2006 in order to meet concrete new demands. we know there will be new demands. we also understood the conclusions of the european council with regard to the future financial perspectives. our common aim must be to have sufficient resources to cover all external relations priorities, bearing in mind the 20% cut in the commission’s proposal for heading 4. in the light of past experience, one particular issue will be to ensure sufficient flexibility to respond to unforeseen needs. i also hope there will be continued support for our stability instrument to enable us to make real progress in crisis response and coherence. this is the main thrust of how we would like to face 2006 and its political challenges. the organizations representing workers in the electrical and electronic equipment industry in portugal complain that over the last three years more than 8,000 jobs have been eliminated by the multinationals operating in the sector, the most serious examples of the reduction in employment levels being lear, vishay, philips, yazaky saltano, alcoa fujikura and delphi. the situation will tend to worsen if the new threats of transfer orders and relocation of companies, which would lead to the unemployment of more than 6,000 workers, materialize. the process of genuine blackmail by multinationals against workers, particularly in terms of the devaluation of wages, the flexibility of working hours, the precariousness of working relationships, among other examples, imposes measures long advocated to stop this genuine race for maximum profit and maximum exploitation, with total disregard for its social consequences and, incomprehensibly, sometimes supported by community financial resources.
the lisbon strategy and its revision have been discussed here in the last two days. it is a matter of the utmost importance. the debate was attended by members of the national parliaments and undoubtedly drew attention to the situation in the various member states. it is essential that the commission and the council now take account not only of the reality in each of the member states, where unemployment continues to rise and high levels of poverty and social exclusion persist, so that the objectives announced six years ago at the lisbon summit can in fact be a reality, but also that a break with the neo-liberal policies of privatisation, liberalisation and the bolkenstein proposal for a directive is needed so that the improvement of economic and social conditions and greater economic and social cohesion in the european union are effectively taken into account.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group, violence against women, ranging from human trafficking to prostitution and domestic and workplace violence, is arguably the most serious. domestic violence is the most common form of violence and affects millions of women in the european union. the rapporteur, who is very much appreciative of her work, has presented some figures here, although it is known that there are no studies at community level. it is imperative, commissioner, that the necessary measures be taken as soon as possible to make this phenomenon more visible, because it is unacceptable that every year more than 100,000 women and many children continue to die as victims of violence in the european union, another area that must be taken into account. i hope, therefore, that after this debate nothing will remain the same, that the reinforcement of the instruments that have already been promised here will be a fact, that the measures will be put into practice and that there will be political will to change this situation effectively.
the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the commission's report on equality between women and men in the european union takes stock of progress made in gender equality, but concludes that much remains to be done to end all forms of discrimination and to ensure that women share in public and private life on an equal footing with men. this requires ensuring a balance between family and working life, strengthening the status of women in the labour market, increasing childcare and other dependent care facilities and mainstreaming a gender perspective in immigration and integration policies. there are two major challenges that lie at the heart of a gender equality policy. one, to eliminate the gender pay gap. the other is the reconciliation of work and family life for both women and men. it is not acceptable that women should be the last to gain access to effective employment and the first to go unemployed, even though they are competent and dedicated professionals. the gender gap in employment is 15.8%, the percentage of parttime employment is on average 30.4% for women compared to 6.6% for men. women with young children have employment rates 13.6 percentage points lower than those of women without children, while men in the same situation have activity levels 10 percentage points higher than their childless counterparts. women do most of the housework and consequently have less time for paid work. in couples with children under six, men do less than 40% of the housework and between 25% and 35% of the childcare. the provision of adequate reception facilities remains a key instrument for enabling women to enter and remain in the labour market. women are needed in all areas of activity, especially in those traditionally considered to be male. it is proven that women are good managers and it is also recognized the creative and innovative capacity of women in city planning and construction. as a successful italian architect once said, men don't wear high heels, they don't ride in strollers, and so they don't plan well-sized tours, and they don't worry about architectural barriers. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i shall take the time available to share some concerns which merit consideration. it is the duty of the elected to read the signs so that they can prevent more serious situations. there has been a lot of talk in the last report about domestic violence and i would like to draw attention to youth violence and its increase. the images of recent events in france have spread around the world, leaving many wondering what drives hundreds of young people to use violence to draw attention to their problems. families, governments and societies as a whole need to look at each other and see where they have failed and why. but it's not just in france. everywhere there is a high degree of violence among young people. it's a very serious problem. what motivates youths between the ages of 13 and 17 to mistreat and even kill defenseless people as a form of entertainment? the facts reported are shocking. a group of youngsters robbed beggars and immigrants just for fun and recorded the whole thing with their cell phone cameras to show their friends at school. another group poured gasoline on a homeless woman and set her on fire. the woman, aged 50, was burned to death. our consciences cannot remain indifferent to such cruelty. but it is not enough to denounce, we must act! so that we do not come to regret it later and say as a father to one of these young people: i feel like a failure as a father! the experts point out the causes. the first of which is the absence of parents. there are thousands of young people in the european union who have been exposed to television, the internet and the street since they were children. parents spend more than 12 hours away from home, leaving their children unaccompanied, at the mercy of all kinds of negative influences, which leads to academic failure, early school leaving, laziness, drug use and marginalization. the second cause is idleness. without any occupation, without school and without work, young people become irresponsible. add to all this a permissive culture with few or no duties and all rights. strictness and rigor are not cultivated, work and merit are not valued. i would like the commission, the council and the european parliament to look into this matter and take appropriate action while there is still time. i hope that the next commission report will contain further progress on equality and i would also like to thank the support of my colleagues and the secretariat of the women's committee in the preparation of this report.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i would like to thank you for your report. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr ferber, on the quality of his report, which clarifies the social and economic importance of postal services in the face of unemployment prospects and signs of concentration. i think it is necessary to prevent liberalization from turning this public service into a purely economic service where only certain sectors of society of the most prosperous can exercise the simple right to send a letter, while the provision of the universal service is not guaranteed to the most disadvantaged and geographically isolated. i therefore suggest that the commission, in future analyses of the sector, prepare a modulation in relation to the costs of financing the universal service, taking account in particular of geographical and demographic constraints, in order to ensure that everyone has access to this service of general interest. as rapporteur, i believe that competitive postal services are fundamental to the european union, positively influencing various sectors of society such as trade, services and employment, through the modernisation of investments that can increase competitiveness, quality and efficiency, allowing lower prices for citizens and businesses and making a decisive contribution to the pursuit of the objectives of the lisbon strategy as a sector capable of generating jobs and growth.

in writing. the pcp meps have long been involved, together with the organisations representing road and urban transport workers, in efforts to improve the labour rights of professional drivers so that the legal working hours and rest periods of drivers are respected and so that 'sacrosanct' competition, in its exploitative nature, does not put them at risk. as the trade unions point out, the regulation which has just been adopted, although it may improve working conditions in some countries, falls short of the existing collective labour regulations in portugal as regards the organisation of working time and the determination of minimum daily and weekly rest periods, as well as their monitoring. among other things, the regulation insists on the maintenance of two different concepts, 'driving time' and 'working time', penalising workers. just as the 'new' concepts of reduced rest periods make it more difficult to monitor compliance with minimum rest periods and encourage the overloading of daily and weekly working hours, we hope that the adoption of the regulation will not be used as a (false) pretext to justify further attacks on workers' rights. in writing. the proposal for a directive voted on today in plenary at first reading is generally in line with the process of simplifying internal market legislation advocated by the european commission. the proposal aims to consolidate existing legislation into a single act and to repeal (or deregulate) all existing packaging formats. certain sectors should, however, continue to be subject to the existing rules on the basis of full harmonisation. the proposal states that the mandatory ranges are justified in sectors where community legislation already provides for mandatory harmonised formats: this is the case for wine, spirits, soluble coffee, aerosols and white sugar. the european parliament also stated that the directive did not apply to pre-packaged bread, spreads and tea, products for which national standards on nominal quantities remained in force. all other sectors will be able to manufacture and consumers to buy products in a potentially infinite range of formats. it also considered that other basic products should continue to be covered by mandatory ranges, by way of derogation from liberalisation: coffee, butter, salt, rice, pasta and milk for consumption.
in writing. the european commission's objective of simplifying legislation deserves my support. one of the biggest obstacles to improving the economic efficiency of the member states of the european union is the excess of legislation, the regulatory confusion, what in english is properly called 'red tape'. this simplifying and liberalizing purpose, tempered by the care that has gone into the amendments introduced by the european parliament, partially removing some liberalization where it proved, in a lasting way, useless or even adverse to the interests of consumers, deserves my support here, expressed in my vote in favour.

in writing. the liberalization of postal services is part of the so-called 'lisbon strategy', which aims to open up the sector to private capital, with the ultimate aim of privatising this public service, starting with its most profitable parts and 'obviously' continuing to be supported by public funding (see for example the model applied to the management of hospitals). the struggle of workers in this sector, as well as of the population - see the numerous actions against the closure of post offices and to ensure postal distribution - has succeeded in delaying and even blocking this process in some of its most serious aspects. the report also calls for the eu to take action to combat the spread of the virus and to ensure that the virus is contained in the body. the report does not criticise the current process of liberalisation, nor does it clearly point out its negative consequences, such as the closure of access points, the reduction in daily home distribution or the decline in employment levels. the report does not call into question the completion of the liberalisation of the sector in 2009, advocating openness and the primacy of competition in this sector. that is why we are voting against it.

in writing. we abstained in this vote because, under pressure from the epp majority and the liberals, the commission and the council finally gave in and excluded solar radiation from the scope of the directive. this is all the more regrettable since optical radiation is known to be part of the electromagnetic spectrum, comprising mainly direct light, infrared and ultraviolet rays and lasers. solar radiation is composed of ultraviolet, infrared and direct light. the health effects of these radiations are well known, in particular because they cause, among other things, changes in the immune system, skin diseases, eye diseases, cancers and psychological disorders. many millions of workers in the eu are affected in their quality of life by exposure to solar radiation while working in agriculture, fishing, construction, salt works, quarries and open-air mines, as well as in various leisure activities, etc. so while the directive has introduced some significant improvements in artificial radiation - which is why we will not vote against it - its scope is restricted by not including solar radiation.
in writing. we are faced with a paradigmatic example of how the european decisionmaking process is often hopelessly slow. the proposal voted on today dates back to 1992, although it deals with a subject as fundamental as the protection of workers' health. it took 13 long years for the european parliament's thesis to be vindicated. the text now adopted deals only with workers' exposure to artificial radiation and excludes radiation of natural origin from the scope of the directive, on the grounds that, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, this matter should be dealt with at national level, in accordance with national conditions and needs. i voted in favour of this report because i agree that it is not feasible for the eu to impose on employers in the 25 member states the assessment of the risks to the health and safety of workers exposed to the sun. i believe that this assessment should be made at national level, according to the reality of each country. this directive requires employers to put in place measures to prevent or reduce the risks to their workers from exposure to artificial radiation, in particular through measures relating to the choice of equipment, the design of the workplace and the duration of exposure.

in writing. we know that state aid is an important economic policy instrument for boosting economic, social, environmental and regional development, in particular so that the state can intervene in order to realise its strategic options, ensure the financing of public services and compensate companies that promote so-called 'services of general interest'. with this report, which is markedly neoliberal, the majority in parliament wants to restrict state aid to a 'last resort' solution, with the ideological preconception of reducing paper and state intervention in the economy in the name of the sacrosanct and beneficial 'market economy', and to avoid so-called 'distortions of competition' - which justifies our vote against. the rapporteur supports the european commission's reform proposals to make state aid more dependent on competition, encourage the reduction of state aid and restrict it to horizontal policies linked to the lisbon strategy, for example those related to innovation and r & d.
in writing. this report on the reduction of the general level of state aid to be granted by states aims to direct the granting of aid towards the objectives set out in the lisbon strategy. this challenge requires a significant change both in the state aid rules established by the european union and in the member states' approach. the commission's regional aid rules are also being amended to take account of the principle of 'less state aid and more targeted aid'. i myself, as rapporteur, generally support this action by the european union. i was very pleased to note that the commission has stated in the reform of the new guidelines on regional state aid that the outermost regions of the european union will continue to be regarded as disadvantaged regions, irrespective of their gdp, for the purposes of the compatibility with the common market of the granting of aid to promote the economic development of regions where the standard of living is abnormally low, and that they will also be able to continue to benefit from the granting of operating aid.
in writing. state aid, presented as a solution to correct market failures, often tends, as the rapporteur rightly says, to generate injustice and promote inefficiencies. we are therefore supporting the rapporteur in this matter, as the commission is concerned. it would be illusory and wrong to wish for an immediate end to all state aid. but the fact that over the last few years such aid has been declining - largely because of the european union - is a stimulus to those who argue that an economy which fully respects the rules of the proper functioning of the market produces greater benefits for consumers, producers and workers. in short, state aid is a model which must tend to be replaced by fairer and more effective ways of promoting a real market.
in writing. i congratulate my colleague, mrs herczog, on her important report on the effects of globalisation on the internal market, which i support, particularly as regards the need to create a healthy environment to support small and mediumsized enterprises and to strengthen their position and access to innovation and financial instruments. i also believe that the creation of an internal market in services is a necessary means of increasing the competitiveness of the european union.
in writing. globalisation provides new opportunities through access to the world market, but is seen as a negative by many european citizens given the profound restructuring and relocations taking place in the european production fabric. the eu must meet these challenges without renouncing its historical and social values which are reflected in the fundamental characteristics of existing social protection systems. at the same time, the eu should encourage the competitiveness of european industry by developing a whole range of instruments referred to in the lisbon strategy. with growth of 1% or 2% there is no room for manoeuvre, and so economic reforms are becoming more and more urgent, especially those linked to the liberalisation of markets, in order to consolidate the internal market. finally, in terms of foreign policy, the eu should insist that the future world powers, such as china, india and brazil, develop their development processes on the basis of a balance between social and economic policies.
in writing. the interest and concerns expressed by the rapporteur in the human rights and democracy clause in the european union agreements deserve our attention. ten years after its first inclusion, it makes perfect sense to question the history of both its use and its efficiency. i understand that there is one aspect which i think should be clear from our analysis: the need to ascertain the impact of this provision. it is good that the european union has included this clause and has regarded it as a guiding principle in its foreign policy and cooperation. but if this becomes a mere phrase repeated in all agreements, with no real consequences, particularly in the event of a breach, it will obviously be worthless. the inconsistent expression of good intentions is a source of misunderstanding and failure in international politics.
in writing. the rapid liberalisation of world trade, characterised by lax labour and environmental standards, poses a considerable challenge to the competitiveness of the european economy. the eu cannot and should not compete with economies based on export subsidies, disregard for basic environmental and social standards and violation of human rights. european integration is based on solidarity, respect for human rights, environmental and social standards and sustainable development. the values of democracy, the rule of law and fundamental freedoms are inherent in the european project. the eu has succeeded in imposing 'a human rights and democracy clause' in international agreements with third countries. but i cannot but regret that such a fundamental clause is still absent from the textile agreements. china, as is well known, has been systematically breaking the rules of the game since its accession to the wto in 2001. in this particular case, it would be more than justified for the eu to impose minimum social and environmental standards in successive trade agreements with this partner. in competition, you compete with the same rules for everyone.
in writing. this report does not raise any difficulties with the commission's proposal. on the contrary, it corroborates and supports all the ideas put forward. the maintenance of the shetland box and the solder box is a timely and balanced response to the review of the functioning and effectiveness of these boxes and the consultation carried out on this matter. the recommendations contained in this report will help to uphold the basic principles inherent in the new cfp: the sustainable exploitation of living marine resources while ensuring sustainable environmental and social economic conditions. i am therefore in favour of adopting this report.
we are opposed to this proposal for a directive which seeks to liberalize services. we must not forget that this is one of the most important instruments of the so-called lisbon strategy, its central nucleus, to intensify the liberalization and privatization of public services, to contribute to social dumping and competition between workers for the benefit of economic and financial groups only. the pressure of public opinion, social movements and workers' struggles, including today's demonstration, are forcing some tweaks to its original wording, but the essential objective remains. so, its rejection is essential, to prevent what was prevented from entering through the door from entering through the window. legal certainty and the defence of social, labour, environmental and consumer rights require that it be rejected, and that is what we are voting for.
