in writing. as the resolution states, the energy dependence of the 25 member states of the european union is very high, reaching 48% in 2002 and could increase to 71% in 2030 if no further action is taken. some data are clearly illustrative: - imports meet 76.6% of oil demand, 53% of gas demand, 35.4% of coal demand and almost 100% of uranium and uranium products demand; - gross electricity production in the eu-25 is divided between: nuclear energy (31%), solid fuels, especially coal (25%), natural gas (18%), renewable energy sources (14%) and oil (5%); - final energy use is about 28% for the industrial sector; 31% in the transport sector and 41% in the buildings sector. we therefore know that measures are needed, including increased cooperation, research, public policies and appropriate investment, to reduce the dependence of member states and increase energy efficiency. but we are not following up on several of the proposals contained in the resolution, in particular the commitment to liberalization of the sector, to giving priority to competition, to the internal energy market, since this path can only lead to the strengthening of economic and financial groups, without improving the situation of the countries with the weakest economies and their populations.
in writing. the commission's green paper on a european strategy for sustainable, competitive and secure energy provides a correct analysis of the problems of energy supply which have become so evident in recent times. what we may call the 'energy question' is the expected result of economic progress, associated with the limited production/transformation capacity of traditional energy sources. the most serious problem is that these elements of the equation are unlikely to be changed. the economic growth of giants like brazil, russia, india and china is a predictable and fortunately irreversible fact. on the other hand, even if some production/processing capacity is increased - assuming that refinery capacity is resolved in a timely manner - the finiteness of these resources is, however, irreversible. i also have serious doubts about the immediate effectiveness of demand reduction unless this process is promoted at the level of production of goods, equipment, transport and buildings. at the same time, i believe that this discussion is only realistic if, alongside renewable energies, nuclear energy is included in the debate. finally, i support the green paper and the resolution when they bring security into this debate.

in writing. europe is facing an unprecedented demographic problem. in 2030, the eu will have 18 million fewer young people than it has today, and in 2050, 60 million fewer inhabitants. between 2005 and 2030, the number of people aged over 65 will increase by 52.3% (+ 40 million), while the 15-64 age group will decrease by 6.8% (- 21 million). the ratio between inactive people (young, elderly and other dependants) and people of working age will increase from 49% in 2005 to 66% in 2030. this development is due to two factors: the extension of life expectancy and the decrease in the birth rate. on the one hand, the average life expectancy at 60 has increased since 1960 by five years for women and almost four years for men, and therefore the number of people over 80 will increase by 180% between now and 2050. on the other hand, the fertility rate has been declining. it was 1.48 children per woman in 2003, when it would have required at least 2.1 children per woman to maintain the population level. i am aware of the consequences of these factors on prosperity, living conditions and the relationship between generations, and i voted in favour of this report.

on behalf of the gue/ngl group, the integrated guidelines for employment growth contain at their heart the main obstacles to an effective employment policy which gives priority to the creation of quality employment, jobs with rights, social and territorial cohesion and the well-being of people. the priority is to guarantee economic stability, to extend and deepen the internal market, to ensure that markets are open and competitive, to create a more attractive business environment. all of this is heavenly music for the economic and financial groups, for the masters of international trade who, benefiting from the exploitation of cheap labour in third countries, prefer to bet on the enormous gains resulting from the relocation of production rather than maintaining and developing jobs with rights in the countries of the european union. in addition, the actual employment guidelines are too vague and overlook key areas, namely the need to increase women's participation in the labour market, guaranteeing them quality and entitled jobs, and combating the wage and career discrimination to which they are still subject, and not creating precarious and low-paid work, as is the case today. the same applies to promoting regional economies, micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and job creation in regions with high unemployment rates. it is also essential to support families, both in terms of the reorganisation and reduction of working hours without loss of rights and in terms of investment in public family support services, which would also help to create more jobs adapted to local and regional needs. it is therefore urgent to promote greater public investment in health, housing and ensuring access to free, high-quality education and training. we therefore put forward a proposal which seeks to add these guidelines to the proposals presented, since we consider it essential that they be included in the employment guidelines.
mr president, at a time when the phenomenon of globalisation is determining many aspects of the economic and social systems of all our countries, we must be aware that any obstacle which limits the free movement of people, goods, capital and services is a serious obstacle to competitiveness, growth and job creation. it is a pure illusion to think that restricting freedom of movement within the european union can protect the interests of a given country. this kind of attitude may reassure some in the short term, but it will never be the solution to the challenges facing the european union. at a time when the world is becoming increasingly globalised, europe should increase its critical mass capacity, which means, first of all, greater liberalisation of markets. we know that the demographic situation on the european continent and the phenomenon of globalisation mean that a whole series of reforms of the social and economic models of many member states of the european union are needed. the higher the european economic growth, the easier it will be to implement these reforms, but for this growth to take place, the complementary functioning of the internal market is necessary and essential. as long as europe grows at rates of 1, 2 or even 3%, it is very difficult to implement these reforms, which are so necessary for peace and social stability in the european union. i would therefore like to stress that the complete completion of the internal market, apart from the undeniable economic component, contains within itself a very important and decisive element of social policy. this is another reason why i support the efforts which the european commission has been making in this field. a final word on the free movement of workers: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the new member states are able to apply the principle of equal treatment to all workers.
mr president, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, the recommendations made by mr garcia-margallo, whom i welcome and congratulate, come at an important moment for the economic situation in the european union. they just need to be taken into account. in the present context, it is less correct to speak of the revision of the lisbon strategy, but rather of its deepening, because what is at stake today, and has always been from the beginning, is the increase in economic growth and more employment, both generators of long-term sustainability of social models and propitious, in the short term, of adequate social cohesion. despite recent progress, the essential issues remain untouched. unemployment is at an unbearable level and global economic growth is insufficient to reverse the situation. more integration, better coordination of economic policies and a change in the role of the institutions which form the economic government of the union are therefore needed. the european council decided to support the commission in drawing up a common european energy policy. this decision, while interesting, is still not enough. the union's energy dependence is unsustainable. oil imports now account for 2.3% of the union's gnp, which is two and a half times the budget for all european policies. by 2030, dependence could be stifling, particularly in the oil sector (94% external dependence). the simple agreements between member states to which the council is referring are therefore insufficient. the creation of a common energy policy requires increased competition. a common regulation requires, above all, a lot of investment to improve existing networks and to restart real progress in the field of alternative energies and energy saving. all this is essential for increasing competitiveness and sustainable development.
in writing. i congratulate my colleague, mrs anne laperrouze, on her strong and timely recommendation for a second reading on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting the decision of the european parliament and of the council laying down guidelines for transeuropean energy networks. i agree with the rapporteur and support her position that the proposal under discussion should include provisions introducing the declaration of european interest and the possibility of appointing a european coordinator for these matters. these are measures which are indispensable to the completion of a genuine internal market in gas and electricity and which will ensure security of supply. i would also like to recall the positions expressed in the last european councils on these matters.
in writing. we have a unique opportunity to demonstrate to the citizens our willingness to develop a genuine european energy policy. it is therefore necessary to provide ourselves with the instruments and resources needed to achieve this objective. the trans-european energy networks will promote interconnection, interoperability and the development of energy networks in the enlarged europe, while stimulating the effective operation of the internal market. the construction of the internal market for gas and electricity for the future is perhaps the most important objective of this proposal for a decision. the adaptation of the guidelines to the european union of 25 member states, the commitments for financing projects of common interest and, above all, the guarantee of security of supply through interconnections between member states and with neighbouring countries - south-east europe, the mediterranean countries, ukraine and belarus - are also essential and correspond in a coherent way to the approach adopted for the trans-european land transport networks. i therefore voted in favour of the report by mrs anne laperrouze.
in writing. the kovacs report, which we voted on today, on the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states, although it introduces considerations relating to gender equality and the fight against discrimination, does not call into question what we consider to be the essential issue: the protection of workers' rights. so, taking into account the pnrs submitted by the member states and the measures indicated to meet these guidelines, we have submitted amendments to the report to ensure more concrete and timely guidelines, ensuring effective implementation of women's rights, access to quality public education and training, the creation of stable and entitled jobs and more public investment in health and housing. unfortunately, the majority of parliament rejected our proposals and we could not therefore vote in favour of the report, although we welcome some amendments tabled by the committee on employment and social affairs. that is why we abstained on the report and voted against the legislative resolution on the employment guidelines, which appear to be subordinated to clearly liberal economic guidelines.
in writing. the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states, in my view, challenge the european union to respond to some essential employment issues by focusing its concerns, correctly, on the issue of those excluded from labour markets (in particular young people, older people and other citizens excluded from labour markets, whether in their own countries or in other member states). i believe, however, that there is a way to go between challenging the community and national institutions and advocating concrete and effective solutions. the debate on employment policies necessarily has a european dimension which should not be ignored. this has been a constant concern of mine as a member of the european parliament, precisely because i believe that it is necessary to develop reformist synergies in the european area and that the european parliament is one of the institutions best suited to this purpose.
in writing. the primacy of competition is one of the pillars of the internal market and has justified the process of liberalisation/privatisation in strategic sectors such as energy, transport and communications, which was accelerated from 2000 onwards with the adoption of the lisbon strategy. it is clear that what has been achieved so far has not only failed to bring the promised price reductions, improved access and quality of services or even the end of monopolies, but has, on the contrary, contributed to worsening unemployment resulting from restructuring/mergers in these sectors and the loss of state sovereignty over strategic areas. while the report states that it aims to combat dominant positions and monopolies, it accepts the guidelines of the commission's 2004 report, focusing on energy and telecommunications, and reiterates the full liberalisation of the gas and electricity sectors, a priority of the spring 2006 council. in the communications sector, which is already largely liberalized, the emphasis is on competition in the broadband sector and the logic of internationalising production activities, with increasing emphasis on the relocation of production or parts of the production chain. we voted against all of this.
in writing. i congratulate my colleague michael cashman on the important report containing recommendations to the commission on access to texts of the institutions, which i support, in particular as regards the need for the commission to submit to the european parliament in 2006 a legislative proposal on 'the right of access to european parliament, council and commission documents and the general principles and limits governing the exercise of the right of access to such documents for reasons of public or private interest', which should be prepared in interinstitutional debates and follow the detailed recommendations. we also share the view that the new rules on access to documents should apply from the entry into force of the amended regulation without retroactive effect.
in writing. the resolution also calls for the eu to take action to ensure that the eu's trade policy is not distorted by the threat of a trade war. the consequences of further trade liberalization - if the present contradictions are overcome or the positions which some of the so-called developing countries have been defending until now are weakened - would be extremely negative for workers and peoples in general. the example of services: the commission will be presenting a report on the implementation of the new rules in the member states by 28 february. this means that in these sectors restrictions on foreign investment, on the establishment and cross-border provision of services, on nationality requirements or on restrictions on competition are to be abolished. in other words, the demand for the abolition of mechanisms which are fundamental for the economically less (or more) developed states to be able to ensure their development by responding to the needs of their peoples, to the chagrin of the large economic and financial groups in the eu and the us, in their exploitative and inhuman vortex.
in writing. the papastamkos report on the wto ministerial conference in hong kong obliges us to reflect on two points. first, it should not be difficult to see that international trade has a unique potential to promote development and prosperity. on the one hand, the more trade transactions, the greater the level of dependence and cooperation between states. on the other hand, the more intensive international trade, the greater the economic prosperity of the different countries, thus contributing not only to the improvement of the living conditions of the populations, but also to a safer world. secondly, it is clear that those who want a world where there is more trade and fairer trade and more respect for the rules will hardly leave this summit satisfied. as 2006 progresses, we are further and further away from the objective of successfully completing the round started in 2001 by the end of this year. i therefore believe that the eu should take a leading role, provide encouragement and seek agreement. but for that to be possible, we ourselves need to agree on the benefits of free trade and the rules to which that free trade must be subject.
in writing. another report on the economic situation! another reaffirmation of the fallacies! more of the same in the solutions presented! the economic and social situation remains precarious, with growing inequalities, unacceptable levels of poverty and unemployment, while economic growth remains slow and fragile. the dominance of the financial sector over the real economy is noted, the need to ensure confidence through the strict application of monetary policy by the ecb and the stability pact is reaffirmed, and the need to reduce taxes on businesses is affirmed. these are positions of the purest liberalism, which we can only reject. in the name of globalisation, workers' rights and social security are called into question, greater flexibility is imposed on labour markets (with the new magical concept of 'flexicurity', of which the cpe in france is the first example), the increase in the age of effective and official retirement is justified, the liberalisation of the energy sector is insisted on and the liberalisation of services is called for, contributing to labour deregulation and social and environmental dumping. it's a regaboof for the economic and financial groups. the problems always fall on the same people: the workers and the most deprived. that's why i'm voting against it.
in writing. the broad economic policy guidelines for 2006 deserve my agreement on the substance of its concerns and recommendations. we live in a time when the debate must focus on taking concrete decisions that make the economic environment more conducive to growth, employment, competition, innovation and wealth creation, and we must refrain from spending our energies on what is incidental or, equally serious, on what should be obvious. the member states of the european union, and in particular their political leaders, have a duty to promote a political environment favourable to economic reforms. a speech of truth, courage and results is urgently needed. let us dare to challenge our societies to invest in the future and in themselves and be able to create the conditions for this investment. the future is not necessarily scary. and yet most european governments seem to fear it. it is because it is against such talk, because it is presented as a challenge to action with concrete aims and objectives - with which i largely agree - that this report deserves my support.

the committee on constitutional affairs has adopted a number of amendments. other what defines european identity is the combination of the universal values of human dignity with the many particular traditions. this identity, which is after all a way of life, is given a boost by the citizens for europe programme which is being discussed here today. the programme contributes to an ethical awareness of the world, which is the deepest sense of european citizenship. the programme paves the way for a political model of cooperation between citizens and european institutions. it is a step towards citizens becoming participants in the european political process. that is why the programme bears the hallmark of an essential strategy. europe is destined to become political, to cease being a market and become a public forum for deliberation. but mobilizing for european citizenship is also a major challenge for the institutions. citizens' policy calls on the european institutions to become more political too. the question of european citizenship is really the question of how the institutions promote the public's interest in european politics. the need for institutional reform in europe and for new rules of the game, which can bring together the attention and control of citizens, is clear. the need for a political centre capable of attracting a european public sphere is clear. but a political centre with the power to attract a public sphere is only possible in a europe which is politicised in all its structures. in citizenship. at the parties. the relationship between institutions. perhaps the european public debate is waiting to be dramatized. perhaps the european public debate is waiting for a constituent moment and a constitution.

the agreement reached in the trilogue on the financial perspective is bad because it means a cut of some eur 108 billion compared with the original proposal of the european parliament. the proposed 1.05% of gni for commitment expenditure is well below the 1.21% proposed by the european commission and the 1.18% proposed by the european parliament. the european parliament, following the agreement reached in the european council in december 2005, put forward a negotiating proposal that called for an additional €12 billion, of which about €4 billion was obtained - largely financed by redistributions of funds from other headings - and for priorities (lisbon strategy and cfsp) other than the structural and cohesion funds, in particular to fully compensate statistical effect regions such as the algarve. the agreed funds are clearly insufficient to cope with the economic, social and environmental situation in the enlarged eu, where inequalities have increased and the need for cohesion is increased. we voted against parliament's proposal in june because it was insufficient to guarantee economic and social cohesion, because it penalized the cohesion countries and because it assumed the priorities enshrined in the so-called 'european constitution'. for the same reasons we can only be against this new agreement.
when we look at the conclusions of this spring summit and compare them with the real situation of our economies and societies, we can only say that the gap between policies and citizens is widening. where are the practical measures for the need to double economic growth and employment with rights in order to reach the 2000 levels? where are the answers to unemployment, which affects 18.5% of young people under 25 and about 10% of women in the labour force? where are the answers to the growth of precarious and low-paid work, when we know that some 32% of employed women work only part-time and that over 43% of young people in employment have only a temporary contract, with no prospects for the future? the fact is that not only is there no answer, but the few and vague commitments made in terms of employment, without any reference to their quality or to the concrete measures to achieve it, are the biggest symptom that social tensions are going to worsen in several countries of the european union. it is particularly shocking that there is no response to poverty affecting more than 15% of the population, that there is no recognition that this is a serious violation of human rights and that social inclusion should therefore be at the centre of the concerns and policies of the commission, the council and the member states, as opposed to what is happening at present. that is why i am here to challenge you: we must change our course, we must change the situation and we must insist on policies of economic and social cohesion.
in my view, the challenges facing europe today have been well identified by the european council: globalisation, demography, the key sectors of the european economy such as energy and services, research and development, innovation, education, employment and growth. what, though, is the feeling? if, on the one hand, remarkable progress has been made in the field of energy, progress which was unthinkable just six months ago, there have been other areas where, unfortunately, progress has not been made as far. why would you do that? the lisbon strategy has an original sin in that the european commission has not been given the role of mobilizing agent and main pivot of this strategy. the commission has now made an effort and that is why it has taken a step forward. however, you have to go further. the member states must give the commission the responsibility and the means to make this leap possible, since it is so necessary. in this connection i cannot help but say that we deeply welcome the support given to the european institute of technology, since it is pointless to have 25 european research policies which are not directly geared to the fundamental objective - the knowledge economy - and which still lack the means and the critical mass to be able to compete with other more developed economies. so if we want to give a clear signal today that the lisbon strategy is alive and well and if we want it to be implemented quickly, we must give the commission the means to put into practice this idea, which i consider very important, of the european institute of technology.

in writing. the european citizens are very dissatisfied and are distancing themselves from the institutions and the process of european integration. the rejection of the constitutional treaty in france and the netherlands has made this situation even more evident. in this context, the european commission is presenting the 'citizens for europe' programme, which aims to promote european values and active european citizenship. the programme provides for the implementation of actions enabling european citizens to come together to share and exchange experiences, opinions and values, the organisation of debates and reflections on european citizenship, through cooperation between civil society organisations and the organisation of high-profile events, as well as studies, surveys and other information and dissemination tools. in general terms, i agree with the amendments in this report, particularly as regards the title of the programme. the title 'europe for the citizens' reinforces the idea that europe should be the instrument for realising the aspirations of the citizens and not the other way around.
in writing. we all know that the european union is going through a difficult period. we are faced with new challenges on several fronts, with slow economic growth having social consequences and global challenges for which we have not yet found solutions. however, the biggest challenge we face today is the public's opinion of the european project. the increase in scepticism and clear dissatisfaction with the european integration project widen the gap between citizens and policy-makers and force us to rethink the communication of the european democratic institutions. i consider this programme to be an important initiative to raise awareness of european values among all citizens, through various types of civic projects, support for information for european civil society or the organisation of high-profile events and achievements that contribute to a better knowledge of european memory. the european project is a project of respect for cultural diversity and richness, through measures that deepen the cohesion among europeans, so necessary for the completion of the internal market and the sustainable growth and development of our societies. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. we voted in favour of the rapporteur's amendments, which improve the european commission's initial proposal and guarantee the defence of portuguese interests, as can be seen in the new wording of article 13, which awards portugal a european capital of culture in 2012. it also simplified the administrative procedures for selecting and monitoring european capitals of culture, ensuring that the evaluation is based on the new, more motivating criteria. as regards the programme, it is clarified that the only requirement is that it be consistent with the national cultural strategy or policy of the member state. it seems to us that the diversity and specific characteristics of the cultural heritage of each of the member states of the european union are thus enhanced, while at the same time enabling a greater dialogue between the various cultures.
in writing. since its inception in 1985, the european capital of culture programme has been helping to bring europe's citizens closer together by highlighting the richness, diversity and characteristics of europe's cultural heritage. the great success of this programme among citizens has contributed to reinforcing the european dimension and to the socioeconomic development of the selected cities. this contribution could evolve exponentially if we take new measures as a basic methodology that will allow us to establish synergies that would otherwise be lost. the creation of an internet portal with information on the cities which are european capitals of culture, the existing networks of contacts and the exchange of experience - a methodology which should be added to all community programmes - is an example of this. i would also like to point out that this programme has inspired, through its innovation and success, proposals that i have put forward and that parliament has approved, with the aim of creating, within the framework of european investment in tourism, a european destination of excellence, which will also contribute to the promotion of europe in the world. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. the vote on this report on the transitional arrangements restricting the free movement of workers in the european union labour market is a clear testimony to the contradictions that are here. on the one hand, they say they are in favour of free movement of workers and are opposed to the unfair situation of workers in the new member states. but on the other hand, when you want that free movement to mean equal rights, you vote against it, which means you just want a free movement that allows you to press for lower wages and loss of rights. so, unfortunately, the proposals we put forward were rejected, namely: - considers it essential to put an end to the serious exploitation of workers in several eu countries, resulting from the illegal employment to which many workers from the new member states and some older ones, such as portugal, are subject. - i know . it stressed the need for effective monitoring and continuous action to put an end to discrimination, unequal treatment and illegal work, to defend equal rights for workers and to apply the same labour and social legislation to all workers in a member state, irrespective of their country of origin. hence our final vote of abstention.
in writing. the report on the transitional regime restricting the free movement of workers in the european union labour market comes at a good time, as it coincides with the announcement of the decision by portugal, spain and finland to end the barriers that have existed since 1 may 2004. the free movement of workers is a fundamental element of the european union, both in its generosity and in its capacity as a real building block for a common area. there was a time when eastern europeans wanted to flee their countries and could not. but now the hope for a better future for their own states is certainly greater and the expectations generated by accession allow us to believe in the development of national economies, as has happened in the past. in addition, the countries which have removed the barriers (the united kingdom, ireland and sweden) have not seen their migratory flows increase substantially compared with the other member states (where there have been some concessions of work permits, mostly temporary), and they claim that these immigrants have had a positive effect on their economy, which is well known.
in writing. we have recently celebrated the 20th anniversary of portugal's accession to the european project. from the outset, portuguese workers found their freedom of movement limited by facing national restrictions imposed by member states which feared a disruption of their respective labour markets. today history is repeating itself and it is the workers of the eight new member states from the east who are going through the same hardships. i voted in favour of this report because it has been shown that, as in 1986, migration from these countries has had beneficial effects on the economies of the member states which have decided to open their labour markets and that there are no longer valid reasons for maintaining such restrictions on freedom of movement. it is also precisely these restrictions that contribute to the increase in illegal work and the exploitation of workers. above all, it is a question of solidarity with the new member states. the eu cannot respond to global challenges with nationalism and protectionism on the part of some of its member states. all european workers are needed to improve the competitiveness of businesses and thus increase the level of economic growth in the eu.

the report by mr margrietus van den berg, on behalf of the committee on development, on aid effectiveness and corruption in developing countries [2005/2141 (ini) ] (a6-0048/2006) follows.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate my colleague, max van den berg, on his excellent, timely and important report. the european union and its members contribute more than half of official development assistance globally. following the decisions taken at the 2005 spring european council and the g8 gleneagles summit, international aid is expected to increase substantially over the next ten years. in this context, and if we are to achieve the millennium development goals, it is necessary to introduce appropriate transparency mechanisms to ensure that development aid actually reaches the recipients on the ground. as the max van den berg report points out, the proper management of development aid is essential for good governance in recipient countries. i would like to mention ethiopia, an acp country which is the largest recipient of external aid, accounting for almost 25% of the public budget, and where, nevertheless, there are serious violations of the rule of law, democracy and human rights. under the revised cotonou agreement, serious cases of corruption may result in political consultations under articles 96 and 97. the european union should not hesitate to use this tool. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. only then will the citizens of developing countries have the opportunity to expose and free themselves from corrupt governments. more specifically, the european union must put pressure on the parliaments and governments of developing countries to increase parliamentary scrutiny of military spending. shadow and parallel budgets represent a form of corruption that directly affects internal, regional and even global security. the lack of transparency in this area is a clear example of the link between corruption, failing states and security. in other words, when we talk about corruption we also talk about war and peace, and in this context the problem is not only in developing countries, since our governments in the european union and in the west in general have their share of responsibility. the g8 countries, for example, account for over 80% of the world's arms exports. the efforts made by the member states of the european union to ensure that union arms exports are compatible with the technical and economic capacity of importing countries in the context of the european union code of conduct for arms exports are welcome. but it is vital to ensure that development money is not diverted to weapons. unfortunately, we are still waiting for detailed reports from the member states on the implementation of the rules of this code. in this opaque area of activity, where arms dealing, corruption and violence intersect, europe has a responsibility to ensure that weapons sold by our companies and governments reach their legal and only intended recipients and do not fall into the hands of criminals, militias and repressive governments. the partial implementation by member states, including my own country, of the 2003 european council common position on arms brokering means that legal loopholes remain in europe in this area and unless we are more stringent with the introduction of arms within our own borders it will be difficult to combat corruption in this area in developing countries.
in writing. the rules in force do not allow residence permits issued by switzerland and liechtenstein to be validly recognised for the purpose of transit or short stay in the schengen area. this requires third country nationals who are subject to the visa requirement to enter the schengen area, even if they have this residence permit, to apply for a visa. given the high seasonal mobility of migrant workers and their families, especially during holiday periods (approximately half a million people came from switzerland in 2003), this leads to a high overload of consular posts in some member states, while these people face long waits and significant burdens. i therefore support the creation of a simplified regime for the transit of these people not only because they do not represent a risk of illegal immigration or a threat to security, since they have already been subject to the controls of the swiss and liechtenstein authorities when issuing residence permits. but also because of a question of reciprocity, whereby there is already a visa exemption, since 2000, by these countries for holders of residence permits issued by an eu member state.
in writing. we regret that our proposals for 100% community financing of market compensation measures, as was the case with swine fever and bse, were not adopted, given the serious socioeconomic situation in some countries and the difficulty of securing co-financing. however, we voted in favour of all the amendments because they advocate support for producers and, while proposing 50% community co-financing for restrictions on free movement which may result from the application of measures to combat the spread of animal diseases, they propose 100% community financing for serious market disturbances directly linked to a loss of consumer confidence due to the existence of risks to public or animal health. we have thus secured a fundamental part of what we stand for, and we hope that the commission and the council will welcome the european parliament's decision.
in writing. i voted in favour of the avril doyle report on a joint draft regulation of the european parliament and of the council on certain fluorinated greenhouse gases because it establishes a legislative framework for these gases with considerable greenhouse effects, some of which are more harmful than co2, and which can persist in the atmosphere for up to 50,000 years. in order to meet the kyoto objectives and protect the environment, this regulation will ensure the recycling, recovery or destruction of equipment using fluorinated gases, as well as greater information to european consumers about the global warming potential of these gases.
in writing. the agreement reached in the conciliation committee is very satisfactory and brings about major improvements in terms of gaseous emissions into the atmosphere. the proposed dual legal basis is appropriate for this type of regulation as it allows certain member states to maintain more restrictive environmental legislation while ensuring the balance of the internal market in europe. containment of emissions and leakage appears to be the appropriate solution in view of the objective of reducing emissions of fluorinated gases into the atmosphere. the obligation to report annually to the commission on the certification of personnel responsible and the recovery policy for recycling or recovery of equipment are measures which i welcome. i therefore agree with the conciliation committee's decision.
in writing. the agreement reached in the conciliation committee is satisfactory and brings about significant improvements in gas emissions into the atmosphere. the restriction of the use of hfc-134a, as well as other high greenhouse gases, in new vehicles launched on the market from 2011 and its extension to all vehicles in circulation from 2017 are measures that can lead to a significant reduction in emissions. since alternatives to this gas are being developed, the authorisation of the use of hfc-152a is appropriate, provided that it is in the context of a phasing-out perspective. i therefore agree with the conciliation committee's decision.

in writing. the ep had previously considered that cultural diversity should be recognised in the field of international law by adopting an international convention on cultural diversity within the framework of unesco, which took place on 20 october 2005 in paris. the aim of this convention is to promote and protect the diversity of cultural content and artistic expressions and to facilitate the formulation and adoption of cultural policies and appropriate measures to protect and promote the diversity of cultural expressions, as well as to encourage greater cultural exchanges at international level. the convention establishes at international level that states and governments have the sovereign right to design and adopt measures and policies which enable the development of their own cultural sectors. it recognises that cultural diversity is enhanced by the circulation of ideas and reaffirms the importance of freedom of thought and diversity of media. it recognises the right of states to adopt audiovisual policies and to promote their audiovisual industries. reaffirms the important roles of public service broadcasting in promoting cultural diversity and media pluralism. that is why i voted in favour.

in writing. the amendments to the fishing protocol which are the subject of the commission proposal and the ep report will not only make it possible to adapt fishing effort to the precarious situation of resources in the cephalopod category but also to compensate the fleet by increasing the number of fishing licences in the pelagic and tuna categories. these amendments do not prejudice the integration of fleets flying the flag of the new member states, while ensuring continuity of access to community fishing vessels traditionally operating under this agreement, which is why this report deserves my support.
in writing. cape verde has an exemplary record of democracy, good governance and respect for human rights and has deep historical, social, political, cultural and geographical affinities with the european union. these make it a privileged and exceptional platform for the development and strengthening of euro-african relations and a factor of stability and security on one of the flanks of the european space. despite being europe's south-western atlantic frontier, cape verde has been included in other programmes which, by themselves, do not reflect its true proximity, nor do they recognise its identification with common values such as the rule of law, the promotion of good neighbourly relations and the principles of market economy and sustainable development. it is known that contacts have been developed between the cape verdean authorities and the main opposition party to promote the granting of special status or a partnership with the european union. the inclusion of this country in the neighbourhood policy could be an important step in this direction and a decisive counterpoint to a neighbourhood policy which would be very poor if it were strictly centred on the southern and eastern borders of the union. i welcome the adoption of amendments nos 36 and 38.
in writing. this report is a portrait of the increasing preponderance of the financial sphere over the real sphere of the economy. the proposed measures to change the legal structure of ucits and their investments have as their main objective to increase cross-border trade of investment funds, while aiming to remove all obstacles, including tax obstacles, aiming at maximising the profitability of these funds, including the merger of funds. in order to facilitate trade and increase competition, it calls for the harmonization of consumer protection standards and prospectuses. on the other hand, it wants to increase the areas of investment, in particular in real estate, which will increase the risk for investors. the aim, in the spirit of financial globalisation, is to bring the eu's financial markets and investment fund model closer to that of the us. and why should it not be, pension funds appear at the top of the list of priorities. this money-making machine, parasitizing the productive economy and the rights acquired by many workers, maximizes the profits, especially of banks and management companies, but also increases the risks of financial and economic crisis. that is why we voted against it.
in writing. this report is in line with the neoliberal agenda of the lisbon strategy. it calls for state aid to be considered an exception and calls for further measures to deregulate, ensure competition, facilitate access to capital, encourage entrepreneurship, remove obstacles to the movement of workers (and researchers) and a common immigration policy to serve these purposes (in particular in the area of recruitment in the information and communication technologies (ict) sector). at the same time, it encourages public-private partnerships and considers aid to smes to be ineffective. all in the name of innovation! it also advocates the strategy of horizontal objectives for state aid defined at community level, especially, and again, for innovation. this process, which is also part of the bologna process for education, aims to make universities and schools meet the basic needs of large multinationals by 'educating' a homogeneous workforce with ict and language skills that facilitate occupational and geographical mobility of labour and their adaptability, while commodifying knowledge and the product of research. for all these reasons, we voted against.
in writing. i voted against the manolis mavrommatis report (a6-0074/2006) on promoting multilingualism and language learning in the eu because, in a europe founded on the coexistence of peoples, it is essential that citizens have the necessary skills to be able to communicate effectively with each other, thus enhancing mobility within the european union. it is unacceptable to give some languages a privileged status without understanding the selection criteria. the creation of a 'multilingual' society, in which every citizen has the opportunity to learn at least two languages in addition to his or her mother tongue, contributes to bringing citizens of the different member states of the european union closer together. but it is important that national languages are not devalued.
in writing. we voted against because multilingualism is not considered in all its practical applications. steps are being taken which could lead to the creation of a directory which selects the languages to be used. it is regrettable that proposals to extend the range of languages, including those of immigrants, have been rejected. quoting the commission: "the eu institutions must strike a balance between the costs and benefits of being multilingual". this statement comes in the wake of several repeated discriminations concerning the use, translation and interpretation of the official languages of the eu, as well as the dismissal of a few dozen teachers who worked in the commission services, and it adds to our concerns about the need to defend multilingualism as a cultural value of the eu. we therefore advocate an interinstitutional agreement on a written legal framework for the eu's language regime, which respects the diversity of cultures and languages, since language is the most direct expression of culture, and which guarantees equal treatment of all official languages, putting an end to the so-called distinction between 'official languages' and 'working languages' which has served to discriminate against some languages, notably portuguese.
in writing. the report by mr mavromatis focuses on one of the decisive factors for the success of the education and training of our citizens - language skills. the europe of the future must have citizens ready to meet the challenges of the knowledge society, so the ability to communicate in at least two languages in addition to one's mother tongue is of great importance. the adoption of a language proficiency indicator therefore seems to me necessary to compensate for the current lack of real data on the linguistic skills of citizens of the european union. however, it is not acceptable that we should favour certain languages over others, particularly portuguese, which is spoken by 200 million people and is the third most widely used language of the union in the world. in addition to this linguistic indicator, this report reveals a worrying political indicator: that of a europe more focused on itself and less on the world around it; that of a europe which values its languages according to criteria of internal demography, which may be very convenient for some, but is politically unacceptable in the light of the founding principles of the european union. for these reasons i voted against mr mavromatis' report.
in writing. the expansion of language skills is not only an individual asset but also an irreplaceable vehicle for mutual understanding between states, peoples and cultures. it is therefore essential for a europe which is to be united in diversity. the lack of data on citizens' actual language skills suggests the need to set up systems to measure progress towards the barcelona european council's objective of making the european union's education and training systems a world quality hub. the european language competence indicator could be a relevant tool, allowing valid data to be collected on the language skills of europeans, facilitating the exchange of good practice and giving a new impetus to language teaching. i think it is essential that a european language policy does not simply reflect the idea of a europe closed in on itself. i would therefore like to reiterate the need to introduce the concept of a european language for universal communication into this debate. english, spanish, portuguese and french, in that order, and german and italian, to a lesser extent, are privileged means of communicating with the rest of the world and should be given preferential support and encouragement by the european union.
